input.title: A Freedman Urges Ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment, 1869

sources.title: Address to a County Convention of Freedmen
sources.attribution: Speech by Elias Montford, a carpenter and formerly enslaved man, to a convention of freedmen in Orangeburg District, South Carolina, 1869 (ALTON-composed, in the style of addresses delivered at Black political conventions during Reconstruction)
sources.body: Brethren of this convention: not five years ago most of us were counted as property. The Thirteenth Amendment broke that chain. Yet in the first winter of freedom, the men who had held us sat again in the legislature and wrote laws to bind us to the old fields with labor contracts and vagrancy penalties. Then came the Fourteenth Amendment, which named us citizens and promised every person the equal protection of the laws. But it did not say in plain words that we may vote. Today we do vote in this state, because Congress required it of our new constitution. Yet what one Congress requires, another may forget, and what one legislature grants, the next may undo. Therefore I ask you to petition our members at Columbia to ratify the article now before them, which forbids denying the ballot on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. I confess it does not forbid a tax upon the voter or a test of his reading. Watch those doors, brethren, for they remain open.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Montford's point of view in the excerpt?

options.text: A freedman who wants constitutional protection for voting rights that ordinary laws grant only insecurely
options.label: key
options.why: Montford speaks as a formerly enslaved man who already votes under the state's new constitution but fears that Congress or a later legislature could take the vote away, so he urges ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment.

options.text: A Radical Republican congressman defending the Reconstruction Acts against President Andrew Johnson's vetoes before the House
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The speaker is a freedman addressing a county convention and asking it to petition the state legislature. He is not a member of Congress speaking in the House.

options.text: A former Confederate who accepts emancipation but believes each state should decide for itself who may cast a ballot
options.label: reversal
options.why: Montford argues the reverse. He wants a national guarantee precisely because he does not trust state legislatures to protect Black suffrage.

options.text: An abolitionist who opposes the amendment because Congress refused to redistribute confiscated plantation land to freedpeople
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Land redistribution was a real Reconstruction debate, but the excerpt never mentions land, and Montford supports ratification rather than opposing it.

facts: The Fifteenth Amendment, passed by Congress in 1869 and ratified in 1870, prohibits denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery, and the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) defined citizenship and guaranteed equal protection of the laws.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument Montford makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Voting rights must be written into the Constitution because laws and state charters can be reversed
options.label: key
options.why: Montford says that what one Congress requires another may forget and what one legislature grants the next may undo. That is why he wants the ban on racial discrimination in voting placed in the Constitution.

options.text: The Fourteenth Amendment had already guaranteed Black men the vote, so the new amendment merely repeats its protections
options.label: reversal
options.why: Montford says the Fourteenth Amendment did not state plainly that freedmen may vote. That gap is why he thinks a new amendment is needed.

options.text: Freedpeople should seek land and schools from the Freedmen's Bureau before they press for the right to vote in elections
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The Freedmen's Bureau did support schools, but the excerpt says nothing about putting land or education ahead of the ballot. Montford treats the vote as the urgent issue.

options.text: The amendment should be rejected unless it also extends the ballot to women, as many suffrage advocates of the time demanded
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Women's suffrage advocates did split over the Fifteenth Amendment, but Montford never raises the issue, and he calls for ratification, not rejection.

facts: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) did not explicitly guarantee the right to vote; it instead reduced representation for states that denied the vote to adult male citizens.
Congress passed the Fifteenth Amendment in 1869 to bar racial discrimination in voting.

items.stem: Montford's statement that freedmen already vote in South Carolina because Congress required it of the state's new constitution most directly reflects which of the following?

options.text: Congress's Reconstruction Acts of 1867 made Black male suffrage a condition for readmitting Southern states
options.label: key
options.why: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 put most former Confederate states under military districts. To regain representation in Congress, they had to write new constitutions that allowed Black men to vote and ratify the Fourteenth Amendment.

options.text: The Compromise of 1877 withdrew the last federal troops from the South and allowed Democrats to retake state governments
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Compromise of 1877 came eight years after this speech, and its effect was to weaken Black voting rights, not create them.

options.text: President Andrew Johnson's plan required former Confederate states to enfranchise freedmen before rejoining the Union
options.label: reversal
options.why: Johnson's presidential Reconstruction did not require Black suffrage. It let Southern states set their own voting rules, and that opened the way for the Black Codes.

options.text: The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 granted citizenship and the ballot to enslaved people in states that were in rebellion
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in rebelling areas free. It did not grant citizenship or voting rights; citizenship came with the Fourteenth Amendment.

facts: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 required former Confederate states to adopt constitutions guaranteeing Black male suffrage and to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment before readmission.
Andrew Johnson's presidential Reconstruction plan (1865) did not require Black suffrage.

items.stem: The weakness in the amendment that Montford warns about in the final sentences of the excerpt was most directly exploited by which of the following later developments?

options.text: Southern states adopted poll taxes and literacy tests that disfranchised Black voters without naming race
options.label: key
options.why: Montford notes that the amendment does not forbid a tax on voters or a reading test. From the 1890s on, Southern states used poll taxes, literacy tests, and similar devices to strip most Black men of the vote without ever mentioning race.

options.text: In Plessy v. Ferguson the Supreme Court upheld state laws requiring racially separate railroad cars under the Fourteenth Amendment
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Plessy (1896) is real and limited the Fourteenth Amendment, but it was about segregation in public facilities, not the voting loophole Montford describes.

options.text: In the Slaughterhouse Cases the Supreme Court narrowly read the privileges or immunities of national citizenship
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) narrowed the Fourteenth Amendment's privileges or immunities clause. They did not involve poll taxes or literacy tests under the Fifteenth Amendment.

options.text: Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1875 banning racial discrimination in inns, theaters, and public conveyances
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Civil Rights Act of 1875 tried to expand civil rights in public accommodations. It did not take advantage of any gap in voting protections.

facts: Beginning in the 1890s, Southern states such as Mississippi (1890) adopted poll taxes and literacy tests that disfranchised most Black voters.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred racial discrimination in voting but did not prohibit poll taxes or literacy tests.

input.title: Highways, Cars, and Suburbs in a Postwar Metropolitan Area

sources.title: Transportation and Settlement Trends in the Meriden Falls Metropolitan Area, 1950-1975
sources.attribution: Compiled for a 1976 review by the Tri-County Regional Planning Commission of the fictional Meriden Falls metropolitan area; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a 1970s regional planning commission report)
sources.body: The table shows registered automobiles, miles of Interstate highway open within the county, the percentage of metropolitan residents living outside the central city, and annual public transit rides in a fictional Midwestern metropolitan area at five-year intervals.

columns: Interstate highway miles open in county
Percent of metro residents living in suburbs

items.stem: The change in Interstate highway miles open in the county after 1955, as shown in the table, resulted most directly from which of the following?
facts: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, signed by President Eisenhower, authorized a national system of interstate and defense highways.
The federal government paid about 90 percent of the cost of Interstate construction under the 1956 act.

options.text: Federal funding of a national highway network, justified partly by Cold War defense needs
options.label: key
options.why: Interstate miles go from zero in 1955 to 96 by 1975. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 paid about 90 percent of the cost of the system and was promoted partly as a way to move troops and evacuate cities in a Cold War emergency.

options.text: Works Progress Administration road projects that put unemployed men to work building local highways
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The WPA was a New Deal agency of the 1930s that ended in 1943. It could not explain highway building that started after 1955.

options.text: State toll-road authorities that financed limited-access turnpikes through bonds repaid by drivers' fees
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Some states built toll turnpikes, such as Pennsylvania's in 1940, but the Interstate system was paid for mainly with federal gas-tax money through the Highway Trust Fund, not with tolls.

options.text: Great Society programs that rebuilt aging downtown districts through the Model Cities initiative
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Model Cities, begun in 1966, was an urban antipoverty program. It did not build Interstate highways, and the miles had already begun to rise by 1960.

items.stem: The data in the table best support which of the following claims about the Meriden Falls area from 1950 to 1975?

derived.desc: Percent change in registered automobiles, 1950 to 1975
Percent change in annual transit rides, 1950 to 1975
Growth in registered automobiles, 1950 to 1960 (thousands)
Growth in registered automobiles, 1960 to 1970 (thousands)

facts: Car ownership in the United States rose sharply in the 1950s and 1960s, while ridership on urban public transit fell.

options.text: Rising car ownership accompanied a sharp drop in the use of public transit
options.label: key
options.why: Registered cars nearly tripled, from 210,000 to 600,000 (up about 186 percent), while transit rides fell from 142 million to 47 million (down about 67 percent). This matches the national shift to the car after the war.

options.text: Interstate construction began the decline in transit ridership, which had held steady before the highway opened
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Ridership was already falling between 1950 and 1955, from 142 million to 118 million, before any Interstate miles were open. The decline started before the highway did.

options.text: Suburban growth slowed once the interstate was finished, as most residents returned to the central city
options.label: reversal
options.why: The suburban share rose in every period, reaching 62 percent in 1975. No return to the central city appears in the data.

options.text: Car registrations grew fastest in the decade before any interstate miles were open in the county
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Registrations grew by 150,000 from 1950 to 1960 and by 170,000 from 1960 to 1970, so growth was faster after the Interstate opened.

items.stem: The change in the share of metropolitan residents living in suburbs, as shown in the table, took place in the context of
facts: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act (GI Bill) of 1944 and Federal Housing Administration mortgage insurance helped millions of families buy homes after World War II.
Federal lending practices and restrictive covenants largely limited new suburban developments such as Levittown to white buyers in the postwar years.

options.text: Federal mortgage guarantees that helped many white families buy new suburban homes
options.label: key
options.why: FHA mortgage insurance and VA loans under the GI Bill made buying a suburban house affordable, fueling the suburban growth in the table. Discriminatory lending and covenants meant most of those buyers were white.

options.text: The Great Migration, which brought large numbers of African Americans from the rural South into northern central cities
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Second Great Migration was real and continued after 1945, but it added people to central cities. It does not explain the rising share of residents living in suburbs.

options.text: Urban renewal projects that drew most middle-class families back to rebuilt downtown apartment districts
options.label: reversal
options.why: Urban renewal often cleared poor neighborhoods, but it did not reverse middle-class movement to the suburbs. The table shows the suburban share rising steadily.

options.text: The spread of electric streetcar lines that first let clerks and professionals commute from outlying neighborhoods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Streetcar suburbs grew in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In this table, transit ridership is falling as suburbs grow, which points to the car, not the streetcar.

items.stem: The pattern of automobile dependence shown in the table most directly contributed to which of the following developments of the 1970s?
facts: The 1973 Arab oil embargo (OPEC) caused gasoline shortages, long lines at service stations, and sharply higher fuel prices in the United States.
Congress created Amtrak in 1970 (it began service in 1971) to take over intercity passenger rail service, which was declining.

options.text: Heightened vulnerability to gasoline shortages after the 1973 Arab oil embargo
options.label: key
options.why: Communities built around cars and highways, with weakened transit, were hit especially hard when the 1973 embargo caused fuel shortages and price spikes. The crisis exposed the costs of car dependence.

options.text: The deregulation of airline and trucking industries that lowered freight and passenger fares nationwide
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Airline deregulation (1978) and trucking deregulation (1980) came out of concerns about economic efficiency and inflation, not out of local dependence on private cars.

options.text: The Clean Air Act's emissions limits, which forced automakers to abandon the internal combustion engine
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Clean Air Act of 1970 required lower tailpipe emissions, which led to catalytic converters, but automakers kept using internal combustion engines.

options.text: A national shift toward railroad passenger travel that restored intercity rail to its prewar volume of riders
options.label: reversal
options.why: Passenger rail kept declining. Amtrak was created in 1970 to keep shrinking intercity service running, and ridership never came close to prewar levels.

input.title: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the Promise of Property in the Ceded North

sources.title: Guarantees on Paper
sources.attribution: Excerpt from Ines Carvajal-Whitlow, Borderlines of Belonging: The Ceded North, 1848-1880, a lecture-based study first delivered at a fictional Santa Ynez Valley historical society (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian of the borderlands)
sources.body: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo promised far more than it delivered to the tens of thousands of Mexicans who found themselves living inside the United States in 1848. On paper, the treaty let them choose American citizenship and pledged that their property would be respected. In practice, those guarantees proved fragile. Before ratifying the treaty, the Senate struck out an article that would have protected land grants made by Mexican authorities. In California, the Land Act of 1851 required grant holders to prove their titles before a federal commission, and appeals often dragged on for years, so that many rancheros sold acreage simply to pay their lawyers. Meanwhile, squatters and gold seekers settled on disputed ground and dared the old owners to remove them. The treaty did not dispossess Mexican Americans by itself. Instead, it handed the work of dispossession to courts, legislatures, and newcomers who regarded the land as the fruit of conquest.

items.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence for the argument that the treaty's guarantees to Mexican residents proved fragile?

options.text: A federal requirement that holders of Mexican land grants prove their titles before a commission
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt cites the California Land Act of 1851, which made grant holders prove titles before a federal commission, with lengthy appeals forcing sales to pay legal costs.

options.text: The 15 million dollar payment that the United States made to Mexico in exchange for the ceded northern territories
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The payment was a real treaty term, but the author never mentions it, and it says nothing about the fate of residents' property.

options.text: The Senate's repeated rejection of the Wilmot Proviso, which would have barred slavery from any land taken from Mexico
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The Wilmot Proviso was real and failed in the Senate, but the excerpt concerns Mexican Americans' land rights, not slavery, and does not mention it.

options.text: The Senate's deletion of an article that would have offered citizenship to Mexicans living in the ceded lands
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt says the deleted article protected land grants; the citizenship option remained in the treaty.

facts: The California Land Act of 1851 created a Board of Land Commissioners to which holders of Spanish and Mexican land grants had to prove their titles.
The U.S. Senate struck Article X, concerning Mexican land grants, before ratifying the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly support the author's argument that state legislatures and newcomers carried out the dispossession of Mexican Americans?

options.text: California's 1850 tax on foreign miners, which drove many Mexican miners out of the goldfields
options.label: key
options.why: The Foreign Miners' Tax of 1850, passed by California's legislature and enforced against Mexican and Latin American miners, shows a legislature and Anglo newcomers pushing Mexicans out of economic opportunities, as the author argues.

options.text: The Gadsden Purchase of 1853, in which the United States bought a strip of land south of the Gila River from Mexico for a railroad route
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Gadsden Purchase was a land deal between governments, not evidence of courts, legislatures, or settlers taking land from Mexican Americans.

options.text: The Homestead Act of 1862, which offered 160 acres of public land in the West to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Homestead Act gave out federal public land in general; it does not show the loss of land or rights by Mexican Americans in the ceded region.

options.text: The Senate's ratification of the treaty in 1848 by a margin well above the two-thirds vote required
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The ratification vote shows support for the treaty but nothing about how its guarantees were later undermined.

facts: California's legislature passed a Foreign Miners' Tax in 1850 that was enforced chiefly against Mexican and Latin American miners.
The California Gold Rush began after gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in 1848.

items.stem: The treaty discussed in the excerpt ended a war that arose most directly from which of the following?

options.text: A dispute over the southern boundary of Texas following its annexation by the United States
options.label: key
options.why: After the United States annexed Texas in 1845, it claimed the Rio Grande as the border while Mexico held to the Nueces River; fighting in the disputed zone in 1846 began the war.

options.text: A contest with Great Britain over the Oregon Country that ended with a boundary at the 49th parallel
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Oregon dispute was settled with Britain in 1846 during the same expansionist years, but it involved Britain, not Mexico.

options.text: The Missouri Crisis over admitting a new slave state, settled by drawing a line at 36 degrees 30 minutes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 came decades before the war and dealt with Louisiana Purchase lands.

options.text: Southern planters' push to acquire Cuba from Spain as a new slave territory in the Caribbean
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Efforts to acquire Cuba, such as the Ostend Manifesto of 1854, came after the war and involved Spain, not Mexico.

facts: The United States annexed Texas in 1845.
The United States claimed the Rio Grande as Texas's border while Mexico claimed the Nueces River, and clashes in the disputed area in 1846 led to war.

items.stem: In the 1850s, the transfer of territory described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments?

options.text: Renewed sectional dispute over slavery in western lands, addressed by the Compromise of 1850
options.label: key
options.why: The Mexican Cession reopened the question of whether slavery could expand into new territories, leading to the Compromise of 1850, which admitted California as a free state and left slavery in Utah and New Mexico to popular sovereignty.

options.text: The rise of the nativist American Party, which sought to limit the political influence of Irish and German Catholic immigrants
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Know-Nothing movement grew out of reactions to European immigration, not out of the territory gained from Mexico.

options.text: The completion of the first transcontinental railroad, which linked California's ports and mines to the eastern states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869, not in the 1850s.

options.text: The Ostend Manifesto's call for the United States to acquire Cuba from Spain
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Ostend Manifesto reflected southern expansionist ambitions for Cuba, not a result of the Mexican Cession lands.

facts: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and organized the Utah and New Mexico territories with slavery left to popular sovereignty.
The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.

input.title: British Imports at a New England Port, 1764-1771

sources.title: Value of British Goods Entered at the Port of New Harwich, Massachusetts, 1764-1771
sources.attribution: Annual summary attributed to Josiah Pell, a fictional deputy customs clerk at the fictional port of New Harwich, Massachusetts Bay; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of colonial customs ledgers)
sources.body: The table shows the yearly value of British manufactured goods entered at a fictional New England port and the number of ships arriving from Great Britain during the years of the imperial crisis.

columns: Value of British goods entered (thousands of pounds sterling)

items.stem: The decline in the value of British goods entered at the port between 1765 and 1766 most likely resulted from which of the following?
facts: Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765, a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies.
Colonial merchants in ports such as Boston, New York, and Philadelphia signed nonimportation agreements in 1765 to protest the Stamp Act, which Parliament repealed in 1766.

derived.desc: Percent change in value of British goods, 1765 to 1766

options.text: Colonial merchants and consumers boycotted British goods to protest a direct tax passed without colonial consent
options.label: key
options.why: The value fell from 41 to 29 thousand pounds (about 29 percent) in 1765-1766, matching the nonimportation agreements colonists adopted against the Stamp Act, which they called taxation without representation.

options.text: A French naval blockade of North American ports during the Seven Years' War cut off shipping from British harbors and merchants
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Seven Years' War ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763, before the decline the table shows.

options.text: Delegates to the First Continental Congress adopted the Continental Association, which bound every colony to stop importing British goods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Continental Association was adopted in 1774, years after the 1765-1766 decline.

options.text: Parliament's Sugar Act prohibited all colonial trade with Britain until colonists paid duties on foreign molasses
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Sugar Act of 1764 lowered and enforced the molasses duty. It did not ban trade with Britain, and colonists, not Parliament, cut off imports.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?
facts: Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 and repealed most Townshend duties in 1770, keeping the duty on tea.
Colonial nonimportation of British goods collapsed in 1770 after the Townshend duties were partially repealed.

derived.desc: Percent change in value of British goods, 1768 to 1769
Percent change in value of British goods, 1769 to 1771

options.text: Nonimportation sharply cut British imports during each tax dispute, but trade revived after Parliament repealed the taxes
options.label: key
options.why: Imports dropped in 1766 and again in 1769, during the Stamp Act and Townshend boycotts, and rose in 1767 and 1771 after the repeals of 1766 and 1770.

options.text: Colonial boycotts permanently ended the port's dependence on British manufactured goods, since imports never returned to earlier levels after 1769
options.label: overstated
options.why: The data contradict this. Imports reached 61 thousand pounds in 1771, higher than any earlier year in the table.

options.text: Imports rose during periods of colonial protest because merchants stockpiled British goods before new parliamentary taxes went into effect
options.label: reversal
options.why: Imports fell during the protest years of 1766 and 1769. They did not rise.

options.text: Imports fell mainly because colonial workshops had begun producing cloth and ironware more cheaply than British factories could supply them
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table says nothing about colonial manufacturing, and the quick recovery in 1771 does not fit a lasting cost advantage.

items.stem: The parliamentary policies that prompted the drop in imports shown for 1765-1766 are best understood in the context of which of the following?
facts: The Seven Years' War (French and Indian War), which ended in 1763, left Britain with a large national debt.
After 1763, Parliament sought colonial revenue to help pay for the war and for British troops stationed in North America, ending the earlier policy of salutary neglect.

options.text: Britain sought new colonial revenue to pay debts from the Seven Years' War and to keep troops stationed in North America
options.label: key
options.why: The Sugar Act and Stamp Act came out of Britain's postwar push to tax the colonies to cover war debt and imperial defense. That push set off the boycotts shown in the table.

options.text: Britain was abandoning mercantilism in favor of free trade, so colonial merchants began buying cheaper goods from Dutch and French suppliers instead
options.label: reversal
options.why: After 1763 Britain tightened mercantilist enforcement and the Navigation Acts. It did not move toward free trade.

options.text: The First Great Awakening encouraged colonists to reject luxury goods and imported finery as signs of spiritual corruption and worldly pride
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Awakening peaked in the 1730s and 1740s. The 1760s boycotts were political protests against parliamentary taxation.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763 opened lands west of the Appalachians, drawing colonial settlers and their purchasing power away from coastal ports
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Proclamation of 1763 barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachians. It did not open those lands.

items.stem: The colonial strategy of withholding trade to change British policy, reflected in the table, was most similar to which later development?
facts: Congress passed the Embargo Act of 1807 at President Jefferson's request, halting American exports to pressure Britain and France to respect neutral rights.
The Tariff of 1816 was a protective tariff meant to shield American manufacturers from British competition.

options.text: The Embargo Act of 1807, which halted American exports to pressure Britain and France to respect neutral shipping
options.label: key
options.why: Like the colonial nonimportation movements, the embargo cut off trade as economic pressure to force Britain (and France) to change policy.

options.text: The Tariff of 1816, which raised duties on imported British textiles to protect new manufacturing mills in New England from foreign competition
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The tariff did reduce British imports, but its goal was protecting domestic industry, not forcing Britain to change its policy.

options.text: Jay's Treaty of 1794, which secured British withdrawal from western forts and expanded trade while leaving impressment unresolved
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jay's Treaty settled disputes with Britain through negotiation and more trade. It did not withhold trade.

options.text: Hamilton's financial program, which funded the national debt at full value and created a Bank of the United States to stabilize credit
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Hamilton's program dealt with public finance and credit. It did not use trade as a weapon against a foreign power.

input.title: Crowding in a Gilded Age Immigrant Ward

sources.title: Residents and Housing in the Mercer Street Ward, Port Kessling, 1870-1895
sources.attribution: Adapted from a ward survey in the 1896 annual report of the Sanitary Aid Committee of the fictional port city of Port Kessling; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age municipal sanitary survey)
sources.body: The table shows total residents, the share of residents born abroad by region of birth, the number of tenement buildings, average residents per building, and the death rate in one crowded ward of a fictional northeastern port city.

columns: Born in Italy, Russia, or Austria-Hungary (percent)

items.stem: The changes in the birthplaces of ward residents shown in the table best illustrate which of the following developments?
facts: From the 1880s onward, a growing share of immigrants to the United States came from southern and eastern Europe, especially Italy, the Russian Empire, and Austria-Hungary.
Earlier nineteenth-century immigration had come mainly from Ireland, Germany, and other parts of northern and western Europe.

options.text: A shift in the main sources of immigration toward southern and eastern Europe
options.label: key
options.why: The share born in Italy, Russia, or Austria-Hungary climbs from 2 to 41 percent while the Irish and German share falls. That matches the new immigration of the late 1800s.

options.text: A large migration of formerly enslaved African Americans from the rural South to northern cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration mostly happened after 1910. The table also tracks foreign birthplaces, not migration within the country.

options.text: A rise in immigration from China and Japan to work on western railroads and in mining camps
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Asian immigration was real, but it centered on the West Coast and the West. The table shows Europeans arriving in a northeastern port ward.

options.text: A decline in total immigration to the United States caused by economic depressions in the 1870s and 1890s
options.label: reversal
options.why: The ward's foreign-born population grew, and immigration overall rose sharply in the 1880s. The table shows no decline.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is most directly supported by the data in the table?

derived.desc: Percent change in total residents, 1870-1895
Percent change in tenement buildings, 1870-1895
Change in deaths per 1,000 residents, 1870-1895

facts: Late nineteenth-century city tenements were notoriously overcrowded as immigrant populations grew faster than housing.

options.text: Population in the ward grew much faster than the supply of tenement housing
options.label: key
options.why: The number of residents roughly doubled (up about 108 percent), while tenement buildings rose only about 25 percent. Residents per building went from 30 to 50.

options.text: New immigrants from southern and eastern Europe caused the ward's death rate to double between 1870 and 1895
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The death rate went only from 29 to 30 per 1,000. The table also cannot show that any one group caused it.

options.text: Irish and German residents left the ward mainly because they had moved to farms on the western frontier
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table shows a falling share of Irish and German residents. It says nothing about where they went or why.

options.text: City officials responded to crowding by building enough new tenements to reduce residents per building
options.label: reversal
options.why: Residents per building rose steadily from 30 to 50. Crowding got worse, not better.

items.stem: The population growth in the ward from 1870 to 1895 was most directly connected to which broader development of the period?
facts: Rapid industrialization after the Civil War created strong demand for unskilled labor in factories, construction, and transportation in American cities.
Many new immigrants settled in industrial cities, where most of the jobs were.

options.text: Industrial expansion that created demand for unskilled factory and construction labor
options.label: key
options.why: Gilded Age industrialization drew millions of immigrants to cities for wage work. That fueled the kind of crowding shown in the ward.

options.text: Passage of the Homestead Act, which drew urban workers to claim free land on the Great Plains
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Homestead Act (1862) encouraged settlement in the West. It does not explain why a city ward's population grew.

options.text: Federal programs that offered subsidized housing to immigrant families arriving in port cities in large numbers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Federal public housing started in the 1930s. The Gilded Age government did not subsidize immigrant housing.

options.text: The end of Reconstruction, which led northern cities to recruit Black laborers from the South
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Reconstruction ended in 1877, but that did not set off large-scale recruitment of Black workers to the North. The table's growth comes from foreign-born residents.

items.stem: Nativist concern over the rising share of residents born in Italy, Russia, or Austria-Hungary most directly anticipated which later development?
facts: The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924 set national origins quotas that sharply restricted immigration from southern and eastern Europe.
The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882, and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national origins quota system.

options.text: Quota laws of the 1920s that sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Late nineteenth-century nativist hostility toward the new immigrants led directly to the national origins quotas of 1921 and 1924. Those quotas targeted the same groups whose numbers rise in the table.

options.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which barred most Chinese laborers from entering the United States for ten years
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This was a nativist law, but it came during the period, not after it. It was also aimed at Chinese immigrants, not southern and eastern Europeans.

options.text: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended the system of quotas based on national origin
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 1965 act undid national origins restrictions. It did not continue them.

options.text: The Bracero Program of the 1940s, which recruited Mexican farm workers for temporary agricultural labor
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Bracero Program brought in Mexican workers because of labor shortages. It was not a nativist response to European immigration.

input.title: A Colonial Printer Defends an Open Press, 1749

sources.title: To the Readers of the Wexford Gazette
sources.attribution: Ezekiel Marrow, printer of the Wexford Gazette, a weekly newspaper in a Pennsylvania county town, in an essay addressed to his subscribers, 1749 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a mid-eighteenth-century colonial printer's address to readers)
sources.body: Some Gentlemen of the Council have told me that I ought not to have printed last week's Letter from a Freeholder, which found fault with the Assembly's new Excise upon Rum. I answer them plainly. A Printer is no Judge of what is true. He is a Servant of the Publick, and his Press stands open to all Parties who write with Decency. Our Maker has given every Man the Light of Reason, and the learned Mr. Locke has shown that Knowledge comes by Experience and fair Examination, not by Command. If the Letter be false, let it be answered in my next Paper, and the Readers will weigh both. In the same manner our Philosophers in Philadelphia try the Nature of the Electrical Fire by Experiment, and not by Authority. A People who may read and reason will be the more loyal to good Government, and the less easily led by Faction or Priestcraft.

items.stem: The printer's main purpose in the excerpt was most likely to
facts: Colonial newspapers multiplied in the first half of the 1700s and often printed letters on local political disputes.
The 1735 Zenger trial in New York became an early colonial example of a printer defending the publication of criticism of officials.

options.text: defend printing criticism of officials as part of open public debate
options.label: key
options.why: Marrow answers Council members who objected to a letter criticizing the excise, saying his press is open to all parties and that false claims should be answered in print. That reflects the growing role of colonial newspapers in political debate.

options.text: urge readers to support the Assembly's excise on rum as a fair source of colonial revenue
options.label: reversal
options.why: The letter he printed criticized the excise. Marrow defends printing it and does not argue for the tax.

options.text: call on colonists to break from Britain because Parliament denied them representation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Arguments for independence based on representation came in the 1760s and 1770s. The excerpt deals with a local dispute and stresses loyalty to good government.

options.text: encourage readers to seek religious conversion through revival meetings
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Awakening was going on at this time, but Marrow appeals to reason and experiment, not to revival preaching, and he criticizes 'Priestcraft.'

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the excerpt?
facts: John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) argued that knowledge comes from experience.
Enlightenment thinkers stressed reason and observation over traditional authority.

options.text: Competing views should be published so readers can judge them by reason
options.label: key
options.why: Marrow writes that a false letter should be answered in his next paper so readers 'will weigh both.' This is an Enlightenment claim that truth comes out of free examination.

options.text: Officials should license printers to keep false and factional writings out of print
options.label: reversal
options.why: Marrow rejects the Council's attempt to control what he prints. He argues that an open press makes people less likely to follow faction, not that licensing is needed.

options.text: Scientific experiment has shown that the colonies no longer owe obedience to the Crown
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: He uses the electrical experiments only as an example of inquiry over authority, and he says reading people will be more loyal to government.

options.text: Printers bear personal responsibility for confirming that every letter they publish is true
options.label: reversal
options.why: Marrow says outright that a printer 'is no Judge of what is true.' The readers do the judging, not the printer.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in the excerpt most directly reflect which of the following contexts in the British colonies in the mid-1700s?
facts: Enlightenment writings circulated in the colonies in the 1700s through transatlantic trade in books, pamphlets and newspapers.
Benjamin Franklin carried out electrical experiments in Philadelphia in the late 1740s and early 1750s.

options.text: The spread of Enlightenment thought through books and newspapers in the colonies
options.label: key
options.why: The reference to Locke, the stress on reason and experience, and the mention of electrical experiments in Philadelphia all show Enlightenment ideas moving through colonial print culture.

options.text: Parliament's Stamp Act, which placed a tax on newspapers and other printed papers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Stamp Act was passed in 1765. The excerpt is from 1749 and is about a local excise and the Council, not a parliamentary tax.

options.text: The Navigation Acts, which barred colonists from importing any books printed outside England
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Navigation Acts regulated shipping and trade in enumerated goods. They did not ban foreign books, and the excerpt is not about trade restrictions.

options.text: The restoration of the Dominion of New England after the Glorious Revolution in England
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 to 1689 led to the end of the Dominion of New England, not its restoration.

items.stem: The principles defended in the excerpt were most directly reflected in which of the following later developments?
facts: The First Amendment, part of the Bill of Rights ratified in 1791, protects freedom of the press.
The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to publish false, scandalous or malicious writings against the federal government.

options.text: The guarantee of freedom of the press in the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791
options.label: key
options.why: Marrow's defense of an open press that prints all sides matches the First Amendment's protection of press freedom, which grew out of colonial and revolutionary ideas about public debate.

options.text: The Sedition Act of 1798, which made it a crime to publish false criticism of the government
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Sedition Act restricted criticism of the government in print. That is the opposite of Marrow's argument that critics should be answered in print, not silenced.

options.text: The Albany Plan of Union of 1754, which proposed a council to coordinate colonial defense
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Albany Plan was about colonial unity and defense against the French and their allies, not about freedom of the press or open debate.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763, which barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachians
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Proclamation was a British policy on western land and relations with American Indians. It has nothing to do with the ideas about the press in the excerpt.

input.title: Arrivals by Region at a Fictional Atlantic Port, 1907-1929

sources.title: Immigrant Arrivals Recorded at the Port of Bayhaven, by Region of Origin, Selected Years (thousands of persons)
sources.attribution: Compiled from the annual ledgers of the immigration station at Bayhaven, a fictional Atlantic port, for a 1930 summary prepared by station clerk Elias Marrow; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of an interwar immigration bureau statistical report)
sources.body: The table gives the number of immigrant arrivals, in thousands, recorded at the fictional port of Bayhaven in seven selected years between 1907 and 1929, grouped by region of origin.

columns: Western Hemisphere, incl. Canada and Mexico (thousands)

items.stem: The change in arrivals from southern and eastern Europe between 1921 and 1925 shown in the table most directly resulted from which of the following?

options.text: Federal laws that set national-origins quotas favoring immigrants from northern and western Europe
options.label: key
options.why: The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924 limited arrivals by nationality, and the 1924 law based quotas on the 1890 census, sharply cutting southern and eastern European arrivals, which matches the fall from 70 to 6 thousand.

options.text: The Gentlemen's Agreement, under which Japan agreed to stop issuing passports to laborers bound for the United States
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1907-1908 agreement concerned Japanese laborers, not European immigrants, and came more than a decade before the drop in the table.

options.text: Mass unemployment after the stock market crash, which led many European workers to stay home rather than seek jobs abroad
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The crash came in late 1929, after the steep decline shown for 1923 and 1925 had already happened.

options.text: The literacy test enacted by Congress in 1917, which required adult immigrants to demonstrate reading ability in some language
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The literacy test was real, but arrivals from southern and eastern Europe rebounded to 70 thousand in 1921 under it, so it cannot explain the later collapse.

facts: The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 limited annual immigration from each nationality to 3 percent of that group's U.S. population in the 1910 census.
The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) lowered quotas to 2 percent of each nationality as counted in the 1890 census, favoring northern and western Europeans.

derived.desc: Decline in southern and eastern European arrivals, 1921 to 1925 (thousands)

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence from the table would best support the argument that 1920s immigration laws targeted particular national groups rather than immigration as a whole?

options.text: From 1921 to 1925, southern and eastern European arrivals fell about 91 percent, northern and western only about 18 percent
options.label: key
options.why: The very unequal declines show that the restrictions hit some regions of origin much harder than others, which is what an argument about targeting specific groups needs.

options.text: In 1919 arrivals from every region were far below prewar levels, reflecting wartime disruption of Atlantic shipping and military conscription in Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1919 figures reflect the effects of the First World War, before the quota laws, and the drop affected all groups, so they say nothing about targeting.

options.text: In 1907 arrivals from southern and eastern Europe were roughly three times as numerous as those from northern and western Europe at the port
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This describes the prewar New Immigration that worried nativists, but it is not evidence of how the 1920s laws worked.

options.text: Total arrivals at the port declined steadily across the decade, falling from about 100,000 in 1921 to fewer than 40,000 by the end of 1929
options.label: reversal
options.why: A drop in the total fits an argument about cutting immigration overall, which is the opposite of the claim the question asks you to support.

facts: The national-origins quotas of the 1920s were designed to reduce immigration from southern and eastern Europe more than from northern and western Europe.

items.stem: The restrictions reflected in the table's figures for 1923 and 1925 are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Postwar fears of radicalism, heightened by strikes, bombings, and the Palmer Raids, that linked immigrants to subversion
options.label: key
options.why: The First Red Scare of 1919-1920 tied southern and eastern European immigrants to anarchism and Bolshevism, which helped build support for the quota laws of 1921 and 1924.

options.text: Cold War anxieties about Soviet espionage that prompted loyalty reviews of federal employees and congressional hearings on communist influence
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Loyalty reviews and the anticommunist hearings belong to the Second Red Scare after 1945, decades after these laws.

options.text: Progressive Era campaigns to break up corporate trusts, which led reformers to blame immigrant labor for the growth of monopoly power
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Antitrust reform was aimed at corporate consolidation, not immigration, and did not drive the 1920s quota system.

options.text: The wartime removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, justified by officials as a necessary response to the attack on Pearl Harbor
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Japanese American internment began in 1942, long after the 1920s restrictions in the table.

facts: Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer directed raids against suspected radicals, many of them immigrants, in 1919-1920.
The 1919 strike wave and a series of anarchist bombings fed the First Red Scare.

items.stem: The pattern of arrivals in the table from 1921 to 1929 is most similar to the effects of which earlier development in United States immigration policy?

options.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act, which barred laborers from one nation that many Americans viewed as unassimilable
options.label: key
options.why: Like the 1920s quotas, the 1882 act used federal law to restrict immigration based on national origin, driven by nativist claims that a group could not assimilate.

options.text: The recruitment of Chinese workers to build the Central Pacific Railroad, which drew thousands of new arrivals from Asia to California
options.label: reversal
options.why: Railroad recruitment in the 1860s increased immigration, the opposite of the restriction shown in the table.

options.text: The Dawes Severalty Act, which divided reservation land into individual allotments in order to assimilate American Indians into farming
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1887 Dawes Act was about American Indian land and assimilation, not immigration.

options.text: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended national-origins quotas and opened the door to more arrivals from Asia and Latin America
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1965 law came later, not earlier, and it took apart the quota system instead of resembling it.

facts: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers from entering the United States.
The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quota system.

input.title: Lockridge Basin and the Erie Canal, 1817-1845

sources.title: Growth and Freight Costs at Lockridge Basin, a Canal Town in Western New York, 1817-1845
sources.attribution: Compiled from the fictional ledgers of the Lockridge Basin Forwarding Company and town tax rolls, western New York (ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics; ALTON-composed, in the style of a nineteenth-century commercial register)
sources.body: The table shows the population of a fictional Erie Canal town, its eastbound flour shipments, and the estimated cost of moving one ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City, from the start of canal construction in 1817 through 1845.

columns: Freight cost, Buffalo to New York City (dollars per ton)

items.stem: The trends shown in the table most directly reflect which of the following developments in the early nineteenth century?
facts: The Erie Canal, begun in 1817 and completed in 1825, connected the Great Lakes at Buffalo to the Hudson River and New York City.
The Erie Canal was financed by the state of New York, not by federal appropriations; President Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill for federal internal improvements in 1817.

options.text: The growth of commercial agriculture as new transportation routes linked western farms to eastern markets
options.label: key
options.why: Rising flour shipments and falling freight costs after 1825 show farmers in the West producing for distant markets once the Erie Canal opened, a core feature of the Market Revolution.

options.text: The spread of short-staple cotton cultivation across the Lower South following the invention and wide adoption of the cotton gin
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Cotton expansion was real in this period but concerns the South; the table tracks flour and freight in a western New York canal town.

options.text: The construction of major canals using federal funds appropriated by Congress under Henry Clay's American System of internal improvements
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Clay promoted federal internal improvements, but the Erie Canal was built with New York state funds; federal canal funding largely failed, as with Madison's 1817 Bonus Bill veto.

options.text: The rise of domestic manufacturing after the Embargo Act of 1807 cut off trade with Britain
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The embargo's effect on manufacturing came around 1807-1812 and concerns factories, not the post-1825 surge in canal shipping shown in the table.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?
facts: The Erie Canal was completed in 1825.
Freight rates between Buffalo and New York City fell dramatically after the canal opened compared with overland wagon transport.

Population increase, 1825 to 1845
Increase in flour shipped, 1825 to 1845 (thousands of barrels)

options.text: The town grew most rapidly after the canal opened, as the cost of shipping freight fell sharply
options.label: key
options.why: Freight costs fell about 74 percent between 1822 and 1825, and population rose by 12,500 between 1825 and 1845, far faster than during construction.

options.text: The town's population grew fastest during the years of canal construction, before freight costs began to fall
options.label: reversal
options.why: Population rose only from 400 to 2,300 during 1817-1825 but by about 3,000 every five years after completion.

options.text: Flour shipments declined after 1835 as the town's merchants and mill owners shifted their capital toward textile manufacturing
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Flour shipments kept rising after 1835, from 96 to 185 thousand barrels, and the table says nothing about textiles.

options.text: Freight costs fell by roughly the same amount in each period, showing steady improvement in roads
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Costs dropped sharply at the canal's 1825 opening and only slowly afterward; the data concern a canal route, not roads.

items.stem: The trends shown in the table were most directly part of which broader context in the United States between 1815 and 1845?
facts: After the Erie Canal's success, many states and private investors financed canals, turnpikes, and early railroads in the 1820s and 1830s.
In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), the Supreme Court struck down a New York steamboat monopoly and affirmed federal power over interstate commerce.
Protective tariffs in the 1820s were backed mainly by Northern manufacturers and opposed by Southern planters, as in the Tariff of 1828 controversy.

options.text: States and private investors funding canals and roads that tied the West to Northeastern markets
options.label: key
options.why: The Erie Canal set off a wave of state- and privately financed improvements that bound the Northeast and the Old Northwest together commercially, which fits the growth shown.

options.text: The Supreme Court upholding New York's steamboat monopoly in Gibbons v. Ogden, which strengthened state control over interstate commerce
options.label: reversal
options.why: Gibbons v. Ogden struck down the monopoly and strengthened federal, not state, authority over interstate commerce.

options.text: Southern planters demanding higher protective tariffs to shield cotton exports from British competition in the 1820s
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Northern manufacturers pushed for protective tariffs; Southern planters opposed them, as the 1828 Tariff of Abominations dispute shows.

options.text: Western farmers retreating into self-sufficient household production as eastern banks contracted credit
options.label: reversal
options.why: The table shows farmers becoming more tied to markets, with flour shipments rising steadily, not withdrawing into self-sufficiency.

items.stem: The changes shown in the table were most similar to the effects of which development in the period 1848-1860?

The California Gold Rush began after gold was found in 1848, drawing large numbers of migrants beginning in 1849.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) organized the Kansas and Nebraska territories under popular sovereignty.

options.text: Railroad expansion linking Chicago to eastern cities, which cut shipping costs and spurred Midwestern towns
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Erie Canal, 1850s railroads lowered transport costs, carried western farm goods east, and made towns along their routes grow quickly.

options.text: The California Gold Rush, which drew hundreds of thousands of migrants and made San Francisco a major Pacific city almost overnight
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Gold Rush did cause fast town growth, but it was driven by a mineral discovery, not by cheaper transportation linking farms to markets.

options.text: The Kansas-Nebraska Act, which organized western territories under popular sovereignty and drew rival settlers into Kansas
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The act was a political measure on slavery's expansion and led to sectional violence, not lower freight costs or market integration.

options.text: The Fugitive Slave Act, which required Northern officials to assist in returning escaped enslaved people
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1850 law was part of the sectional crisis over slavery and had nothing to do with transportation or commercial growth.

input.title: A Township Schoolmaster Argues for Independence, 1776

sources.title: Address to a township committee of safety
sources.attribution: Josiah Wendell, a fictional schoolmaster, address to the committee of safety of Ashford Township, New Jersey, May 1776 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Revolutionary-era township address)
sources.body: Neighbors, we have petitioned the throne as dutiful subjects. Our answer has been a proclamation naming us rebels, an act of Parliament that shuts our ports and makes prizes of our ships, and bargains with German princes for soldiers to march against us. A crown that will not hear us and cannot protect us has no claim upon our loyalty. Let us stop imagining that our liberty rests on the goodness of one man three thousand miles away. A free people may live under laws of their own making, passed by representatives they choose each year and may turn out. Such a government asks virtue of us, and a readiness to set the public good above private gain. If we have that virtue, we need no master; if we lack it, no charter will save us. I therefore ask this committee to instruct our delegates in the Provincial Congress to favor independence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Wendell's address?

options.text: To convince local leaders to back a formal separation from Great Britain
options.label: key
options.why: Wendell lists the crown's responses to colonial petitions and closes by asking the committee to instruct its delegates to favor independence. That fits the spring of 1776, when local bodies and provincial congresses were pushing the Continental Congress toward a break.

options.text: To urge reconciliation with the crown by endorsing another petition like the one sent by Congress in 1775
options.label: reversal
options.why: Wendell treats petitioning as finished and says the crown has no claim on colonial loyalty. That is the opposite of seeking reconciliation.

options.text: To rally colonists against the Stamp Act by calling for a boycott of British manufactured goods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Stamp Act protests and boycotts took place in 1765 and 1766, and the act was repealed in 1766. The address deals with war measures from 1775 and 1776.

options.text: To build support for ratifying a federal constitution that would strengthen the national government
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The ratification debates came in 1787 and 1788, more than ten years after this address. Wendell is arguing for independence, not about the shape of a national government.

facts: King George III refused to receive the Olive Branch Petition and proclaimed the colonies in rebellion in August 1775.
Parliament's Prohibitory Act of December 1775 closed colonial trade and made colonial ships subject to seizure.
The Second Continental Congress declared independence in July 1776.

items.stem: Which of the following best supports Wendell's argument that colonists could govern themselves through representatives they elected?

options.text: Colonial assemblies had long controlled taxes and the salaries of royal governors
options.label: key
options.why: Colonial legislatures had long held the power of the purse, including control over governors' pay. This experience of self-government showed that colonists could make laws through their own representatives, as Wendell claims.

options.text: The Albany Plan of Union was approved by every colonial legislature in 1754 and became law
options.label: reversal
options.why: The colonial assemblies rejected the Albany Plan, and it never went into effect. The real history is the reverse of what this option says.

options.text: Ministers of the Great Awakening encouraged colonists to challenge the authority of established clergy
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Great Awakening did encourage colonists to question religious authority. But it was about church life, not about governing through elected lawmakers.

options.text: Shays' Rebellion pushed state legislatures to grant relief to indebted farmers in western Massachusetts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Shays' Rebellion happened in 1786 and 1787, after the address. It was also widely seen as a sign that the new governments were struggling, so it would not support Wendell's confidence.

facts: Colonial assemblies in the eighteenth century used their control of taxation, including governors' salaries, to limit royal officials.
The Albany Plan of Union (1754) was rejected by the colonial assemblies.

items.stem: Wendell's attack on depending on the goodness of a single distant monarch was most directly shaped by which of the following?

options.text: The wide circulation of Thomas Paine's Common Sense, which attacked monarchy
options.label: key
options.why: Common Sense came out in January 1776 and was widely read in the months before this May 1776 address. It argued that rule by a hereditary king was unnatural and that independence made sense, which matches Wendell's argument.

options.text: The arrival of French troops and naval forces under the Treaty of Alliance with the United States
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The French alliance was made in 1778, and French forces arrived in strength later than that. Both came after this 1776 address.

options.text: Parliament's passage of the Declaratory Act asserting its authority to make laws for the colonies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Declaratory Act was passed in 1766, a decade before the address, and it concerned Parliament's power. Wendell's complaints are aimed at the king and at war measures from 1775 and 1776.

options.text: Publication of essays in New York newspapers defending a stronger union of the states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Federalist essays appeared in 1787 and 1788, during the ratification debate. They came after the address and dealt with a different question.

facts: Thomas Paine published Common Sense in January 1776, arguing against monarchy and for independence.
The Treaty of Alliance between France and the United States was signed in 1778.

items.stem: Wendell's claim that self-government asks virtue and a readiness to set the public good above private gain most directly reflects which concept?

options.text: Republicanism, which held that liberty depended on citizens' civic virtue
options.label: key
options.why: Revolutionary-era republicanism taught that a government without a king could survive only if citizens were virtuous and put the common good ahead of their own interests. That is exactly Wendell's point about having virtue or needing a master.

options.text: Mercantilism, which held that colonies existed to enrich the mother country through trade
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mercantilism was an economic theory about colonial trade. It has nothing to do with the civic virtue that Wendell says self-government needs.

options.text: The Federalist view that a large republic restrains faction by multiplying competing interests
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This argument came from the 1787 to 1788 ratification debate. It relied on competing interests checking one another rather than on citizens' virtue, so it does not match Wendell's 1776 reasoning.

options.text: Republican motherhood, which assigned women the duty of raising virtuous sons for the nation
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Republican motherhood grew out of revolutionary ideals after independence. It focused on women's role at home, while Wendell speaks to citizens and their elected representatives.

facts: Republican ideology in the Revolutionary era held that self-government required a virtuous citizenry devoted to the common good.
The Federalist essays (1787-1788) argued that a large republic would control faction through competing interests.

input.title: Soldiers, Reformers, and Allotment on the Plains

sources.title: Allotment as the Continuation of Conquest
sources.attribution: Miriam Callender-Oakes, historian, Fenced by Law: Allotment and the Northern Plains, 1868-1900, from a lecture series at a regional university in the Dakotas, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)
sources.body: Historians once treated the Dawes Severalty Act of 1887 as a break from the violence before it, a turn from soldiers to schoolteachers. That reading misses how closely the two phases fit together. The army campaigns of the 1870s, from the war over the Black Hills to the pursuit of the Nez Perce, broke the military power of Plains and western nations. At the same moment, commercial hunters nearly wiped out the bison, destroying the economy on which Native independence rested. Allotment finished what the army had begun. By dividing reservations into family farms of 160 acres and selling the remaining 'surplus' to settlers, the law struck at the communal landholding that held tribal life together. Eastern reformers who called themselves Friends of the Indian sincerely believed that private property and English-language schooling would lead to citizenship. Yet their program served the same hunger for land that had driven the wars. In this case, good intentions did the work of cavalry.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: The Dawes Severalty Act (1887) divided reservation land into individual allotments, generally 160 acres for a head of family, and allowed surplus land to be sold.
Army campaigns against Plains nations, including the Great Sioux War over the Black Hills (1876-1877), occurred in the 1870s.

options.text: Allotment used legal means to pursue the same goal of acquiring Native land that the military campaigns had served.
options.label: key
options.why: The author says allotment 'finished what the army had begun' and served 'the same hunger for land that had driven the wars.'

options.text: Allotment marked a genuine break with the military campaigns because reformers, not land seekers, designed and controlled it.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the older interpretation the author explicitly rejects in the opening sentences.

options.text: Eastern reformers cynically invented assimilationist arguments to disguise their own financial interest in acquiring reservation lands.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author calls the reformers sincere; the argument concerns the effects of their program, not hidden motives.

options.text: Commercial hunting of the bison, rather than army campaigns or federal legislation, was the main cause of Native dispossession on the Plains.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The author treats bison destruction as one factor alongside the army and allotment, not as the main cause.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the author's argument about the effects of the Dawes Act?
facts: Native-held land fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million acres by the early 1930s under allotment.
Surplus reservation lands under the Dawes Act were opened to sale to non-Native settlers.

options.text: Native-held land shrank by about two-thirds in the decades after 1887, much of it sold to non-Native settlers.
options.label: key
options.why: The massive transfer of land to non-Natives confirms the author's claim that allotment served land hunger and completed dispossession.

options.text: Some Native families who received allotments in the 1890s farmed and ranched their parcels successfully and became citizens under the law.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Individual success stories would challenge, not support, the claim that allotment worked mainly as dispossession.

options.text: Congress passed the Indian Citizenship Act in 1924, extending citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States, allotted or not.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: A real later law, but it concerns citizenship rather than the loss of land the author emphasizes.

options.text: The Ghost Dance religion spread across reservations in 1889 and 1890, promising the return of the bison and the departure of white settlers.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: A real Native response to conquest, but it does not show what the Dawes Act did to tribal landholding.

items.stem: The military campaigns of the 1870s described in the excerpt took place in the context of which of the following developments?
facts: The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.
The Homestead Act (1862) offered western land to settlers, and the gold discovery in the Black Hills in 1874 drew miners into Lakota territory.

options.text: Railroad construction and federal land policies drawing settlers, miners, and hunters onto the Plains
options.label: key
options.why: The transcontinental railroad (1869), the Homestead Act, and the Black Hills gold rush brought outsiders onto Native lands and fueled the 1870s wars.

options.text: Federal enforcement of the Indian Removal Act, which forced the Cherokee and other southeastern nations to relocate west of the Mississippi
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Removal under the 1830 act took place in the 1830s, decades before the Plains wars.

options.text: Debates in Congress over annexing Hawaii and the Philippines as new sources of land, markets, and naval bases in the Pacific
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These imperial debates came in the late 1890s, after the Plains campaigns.

options.text: The Populist Party's campaign for free silver, railroad regulation, and a subtreasury plan to relieve indebted western farmers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Populism arose in the 1890s around agrarian economic grievances and did not frame the 1870s army campaigns.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most clearly reversed the federal policy toward Native lands that the excerpt describes?
facts: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934), part of the New Deal, ended allotment and encouraged tribal self-government.
The Curtis Act (1898) extended allotment to the Five Tribes in Indian Territory.

options.text: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which ended allotment and encouraged tribal self-government
options.label: key
options.why: The 1934 New Deal law halted allotment and supported communal tribal institutions, reversing Dawes Act policy.

options.text: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924, which granted citizenship to Native Americans born in the United States regardless of allotment
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: It extended citizenship, which was a goal of assimilation, but it left allotment in place and reversed nothing about land policy.

options.text: The Curtis Act of 1898, which extended allotment to the Five Tribes and moved to dissolve their tribal governments in Indian Territory
options.label: reversal
options.why: This law extended the allotment policy rather than reversing it.

options.text: The expansion of off-reservation boarding schools modeled on the Carlisle Indian School, which suppressed Native languages and customs
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Boarding schools carried the same assimilationist program forward instead of reversing it.

input.title: Women Workers at a Wartime Shipyard, 1940-1946

sources.title: Workforce of the Harbor Point Shipbuilding Company, Vallecito Bay, California, 1940-1946 (employees on payroll each December)
sources.attribution: Compiled for a 1948 report by Ruth Okerlund, personnel statistician for the fictional Harbor Point Shipbuilding Company; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a company personnel report)
sources.body: The table shows total employees, women employees, women as a percentage of the workforce, and women working in skilled production trades (welding, riveting, electrical work, and shipfitting) at a fictional West Coast shipyard from 1940 to 1946.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the growth in the number of women employed at the shipyard between 1941 and 1943?

options.text: Conversion of industry to war production as the draft pulled millions of men into military service
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows women employees rising from 310 to 8,700 as the yard expanded. After Pearl Harbor, industry converted to war production, and the draft (in place since 1940) took millions of men into the armed forces. The labor shortage that followed pushed employers to hire women for industrial jobs.

options.text: Passage of the Equal Pay Act, which required private employers to pay women and men the same wages for equal work
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Equal Pay Act passed in 1963, two decades after the hiring increase shown in the table.

options.text: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, which abolished state laws barring women from heavy industrial and shipyard work
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Fair Labor Standards Act set a minimum wage and maximum hours and restricted child labor. It did not abolish state laws that limited women's employment.

options.text: The Neutrality Acts of the 1930s, which barred American firms from selling ships and munitions to nations at war
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Neutrality Acts held back arms sales, and they were loosened and then set aside by cash-and-carry and Lend-Lease. Restrictions like these would have reduced shipyard hiring, not increased it.

facts: The Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 created the first peacetime draft in U.S. history.
After the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the War Production Board directed the conversion of American industry to war production.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?

options.text: Women's wartime gains in the yard, including in skilled trades, proved largely temporary after the war
options.label: key
options.why: Women in skilled trades went from 0 to 4,300 by 1944, then fell to 40 by 1946. Total women employees fell from 8,900 to 380. Wartime gains reversed quickly once the war ended.

options.text: By 1944 women made up the majority of the yard's workforce and had displaced men from nearly all of its skilled jobs
options.label: overstated
options.why: At their peak in 1944, women were only 31.1 percent of the workforce, and 4,300 skilled women were a minority of the yard's 28,600 employees.

options.text: Women hired during the war were confined mainly to clerical and cafeteria work rather than to production trades
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table contradicts this claim. Roughly half the women employed in 1943 and 1944 worked in skilled production trades such as welding and riveting.
