options.text: Women's employment at the yard peaked in 1943 and declined steadily thereafter as war contracts were canceled
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The number of women employees peaked in December 1944 at 8,900, not in 1943. The share of women in the workforce also rose in 1944.

derived.desc: Change in women in skilled trades, 1944 to 1946
Percent change in women employees, 1944 to 1946
Women as percent of workforce, 1944

facts: Millions of American women took industrial jobs in defense plants and shipyards during World War II, including skilled trades such as welding and riveting.
Many women war workers lost their industrial jobs in 1945 and 1946 as war production ended.

items.stem: The change in the shipyard's workforce between December 1944 and December 1946 most directly reflected which of the following?

options.text: Canceled war contracts and returning veterans who held reemployment rights to their prewar jobs
options.label: key
options.why: When the war ended in 1945, the government canceled military contracts and demobilized millions of servicemen. Veterans had reemployment rights under the 1940 draft law, and social pressure pushed women out of industrial jobs. This explains why both total and female employment dropped sharply.

options.text: Passage of the Taft-Hartley Act, which outlawed the closed shop and allowed states to enact right-to-work laws
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Taft-Hartley passed in 1947, after the decline shown in the table had already happened, and it dealt with union power, not with the end of war production.

options.text: A sharp economic depression after the war, comparable to the 1930s, that closed most heavy industry nationwide
options.label: reversal
options.why: No depression followed the war. Pent-up consumer demand drove a postwar boom, even though war industries cut back.

options.text: Federal loyalty review programs that removed suspected Communists from defense plants and naval shipyards
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The federal loyalty program began in 1947 and targeted alleged subversives. It did not cause the general loss of women's shipyard jobs in 1945 and 1946.

facts: World War II ended in 1945, followed by the rapid demobilization of U.S. armed forces and the cancellation of many war production contracts.
The Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 gave returning servicemen rights to reemployment in their former civilian jobs.

items.stem: The pattern of women's employment shown in the table was most similar to which earlier development?

options.text: Women's entry into factory and railroad jobs during World War I, much of which ended after the armistice
options.label: key
options.why: During World War I, the draft and the drop in immigration created labor shortages. Women filled industrial and transportation jobs, and many lost them when the war ended. This is the same temporary wartime pattern the table shows for World War II.

options.text: The steady growth of women's clerical and sales employment in the late 1800s as corporations expanded office work
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Women's clerical work did grow in the Gilded Age. But that growth was long-term and steady, not a wartime surge followed by a reversal.

options.text: New Deal relief programs of the 1930s that gave women a majority of federal work-relief jobs in heavy construction
options.label: reversal
options.why: New Deal work relief mostly went to male breadwinners. Women received a minority of jobs, usually in sewing, clerical, or service projects, not heavy construction.

options.text: Ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, which guaranteed women equal access to industrial employment
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Nineteenth Amendment guaranteed women the right to vote. It said nothing about employment or equal access to jobs.

facts: During U.S. involvement in World War I (1917-1918), labor shortages drew women into factory, munitions, and railroad jobs, many of which they left or lost after the war.
The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, prohibited denying the vote on account of sex.

input.title: Suburban Roots of the Environmental Movement and the Creation of the EPA

sources.title: The Suburban Origins of Environmental Politics
sources.attribution: Delphine Arceneaux-Pryor, historian, Backyard Politics: Suburban Families and the Making of American Environmental Law, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political history of environmentalism)
sources.body: The movement that produced the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970 was less a crusade to save distant wilderness than a revolt of the postwar suburbs. The families who moved into new subdivisions in the 1950s expected clean air, safe water, and open space to come with the prosperity they had earned. By the late 1960s, smog over the freeways, detergent foam in creeks, and pesticide residues in food seemed to break that promise. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring had already taught a wide readership in 1962 to see chemicals as invisible threats to the body. When oil fouled the beaches of Santa Barbara and the Cuyahoga River caught fire in 1969, these worries became televised events. Politicians of both parties raced to claim the issue, and a Republican president created the EPA through executive reorganization. Environmentalism, in this view, was a consumer movement for a healthy home life, and its middle-class roots shaped both its strengths and its blind spots.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?
facts: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, published in 1962, warned of the dangers of pesticides such as DDT.
The Santa Barbara oil spill and the Cuyahoga River fire both occurred in 1969.

options.text: Environmentalism grew largely from suburban families' expectations of a healthy, comfortable life.
options.label: key
options.why: The author calls the movement a revolt of the postwar suburbs and a consumer movement for a healthy home life with middle-class roots.

options.text: Environmentalism mainly continued the Progressive Era campaign to preserve western wilderness and forests as public lands.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author explicitly says the movement was less a crusade to save distant wilderness, rejecting a mainly conservationist interpretation.

options.text: Federal environmental laws were imposed by officials in Washington despite widespread resistance from suburban voters and their representatives.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author argues suburban voters drove the issue and politicians of both parties raced to claim it, the opposite of popular resistance.

options.text: Environmentalism emerged chiefly from industrial labor unions demanding safer conditions inside factories and mines.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about unions or workplace safety; it locates the movement among middle-class suburban households.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would most directly modify the author's argument about the social roots of the environmental movement?
facts: In the late 1960s, the United Farm Workers, led by Mexican American and Filipino American farmworkers, campaigned against pesticide exposure in the fields, and its 1970 grape contracts included pesticide protections.
The first Earth Day was held on April 22, 1970.

options.text: Mexican American farmworkers in the United Farm Workers protested pesticide exposure in the fields in the late 1960s.
options.label: key
options.why: Farmworker activism against pesticides shows environmental concern arising among working-class, nonsuburban communities, complicating the claim that the movement's roots were mainly middle-class and suburban.

options.text: Congress passed the Clean Air Act of 1970 by wide margins, with strong support from lawmakers in both the Democratic and Republican parties.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Bipartisan passage is accurate but supports the author's point that politicians of both parties raced to claim the issue; it does not modify the argument.

options.text: Silent Spring became a national best seller, and its warnings about pesticides were widely discussed in magazines and on television.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true but reinforces the author's use of Carson's book as evidence of broad middle-class anxiety about chemicals.

options.text: Millions of Americans, many from suburban schools and communities, took part in the first Earth Day events in April 1970.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Mass suburban participation in Earth Day supports rather than modifies the author's claim about suburban roots.

items.stem: The expectations of suburban families described in the excerpt developed most directly in the context of which of the following?
facts: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act (GI Bill) of 1944 and Federal Housing Administration mortgage insurance helped millions of families buy homes after World War II.
The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 funded the interstate highway system, which encouraged suburban growth.

options.text: Postwar economic growth and federal housing and highway policies that encouraged suburban growth
options.label: key
options.why: Postwar affluence, the GI Bill, FHA loans, and interstate highways fueled the 1950s move to suburbs that the author describes as the source of environmental expectations.

options.text: New Deal programs such as the Civilian Conservation Corps, which employed young men in reforestation and soil conservation projects
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The CCC belonged to the 1930s Depression era and did not shape the expectations of 1950s suburban families.

options.text: The 1973 Arab oil embargo, which caused fuel shortages and rising gasoline prices that pushed Americans to conserve energy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The embargo came after the EPA was created in 1970 and could not have produced the expectations the author traces to the 1950s.

options.text: The Great Migration, in which millions of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern and western cities
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Migration was a real movement to cities, but the excerpt concerns the growth of mostly white middle-class suburbs and their expectations.

items.stem: The creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970 was significant primarily because it
facts: The Environmental Protection Agency began operating in December 1970 after President Richard Nixon created it through an executive reorganization plan.
The National Park Service was created in 1916, long before the EPA.
The Reagan administration in the 1980s sought to reduce federal environmental regulation.

options.text: expanded federal authority to set and enforce national standards for pollution by private industry
options.label: key
options.why: The EPA brought pollution regulation into one federal agency that set and enforced national standards on industry, a major expansion of federal regulatory power.

options.text: returned responsibility for regulating air and water quality from the federal government to the individual states
options.label: reversal
options.why: The EPA centralized regulation at the federal level rather than handing authority back to the states.

options.text: created the first system of national parks and forests to protect scenic western lands from private development
options.label: misattributed
options.why: National forests and parks came out of the Progressive Era, including the National Park Service in 1916, not the EPA.

options.text: produced a lasting bipartisan consensus on environmental regulation that went unchallenged by conservatives in the 1980s
options.label: overstated
options.why: Support was bipartisan in 1970, but conservatives in the Reagan era challenged and tried to roll back environmental regulation.

input.title: Steel Rails at a Pennsylvania Bessemer Works, 1870-1895

sources.title: Keystone Bessemer Works, Brennan Falls, Pennsylvania: Output, Prices, and Workforce, 1870-1895
sources.attribution: Summary prepared by company clerk Owen Talbert for the 1896 shareholders' report of the fictional Keystone Bessemer Works; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age industrial firm's annual report)
sources.body: The table shows steel rail output, the average selling price of steel rails, the number of workers employed, and the percentage of those workers who were foreign-born at a fictional Pennsylvania steel works at five-year intervals from 1870 to 1895.

columns: Average price of steel rails (dollars per ton)

items.stem: Which of the following most directly explains the trends in steel rail output and price shown in the table between 1870 and 1895?
facts: The Bessemer process, adopted widely in the United States in the 1870s, made mass production of cheap steel possible.
Andrew Carnegie's steel firm used vertical integration, controlling iron ore, coke, and transportation, to cut costs in the 1870s-1890s.
Steel tariffs in the Gilded Age protected American producers from foreign competition.

options.text: New production methods such as the Bessemer process and integrated control of raw materials that lowered costs
options.label: key
options.why: Output rose sixtyfold while price fell about 77 percent, the signature of technological and organizational cost cutting such as the Bessemer process and vertical integration.

options.text: High protective tariffs on imported steel that forced American mills to compete by lowering their prices to world levels
options.label: reversal
options.why: Gilded Age tariffs shielded American steelmakers from foreign competition; they did not push domestic prices down.

options.text: Federal enforcement of the Sherman Antitrust Act that broke up large steel combinations and restored competition among mills
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Sherman Act came in 1890, after most of the price drop, and was weakly enforced; it broke up no steel combinations in this period.

options.text: Rate regulation by the Interstate Commerce Commission that reduced the freight costs mills paid to ship iron ore and coal
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The ICC, created in 1887, had little effective power and does not explain price declines that began in the 1870s.

derived.desc: Percent change in steel rail price, 1870 to 1895
Ratio of 1895 output to 1870 output

items.stem: A historian argues that the falling price of steel rails shown in the table depended partly on reducing labor costs. Which evidence would best support this argument?
facts: In the 1892 Homestead lockout, Carnegie Steel defeated the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers.
Many steelworkers in the late 1800s worked twelve-hour shifts.
The Haymarket affair of 1886 damaged the reputation of the Knights of Labor.

options.text: Steel firms imposed wage cuts and twelve-hour shifts, as in the 1892 Homestead lockout that broke a union
options.label: key
options.why: Wage cuts, long shifts, and the defeat of the Amalgamated Association at Homestead show labor costs being driven down, which directly supports the historian's claim.

options.text: The number of workers employed at the works rose roughly ninefold between 1870 and 1895, keeping pace with the growth of output
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The table does show more workers, but a larger workforce says nothing about lower pay per worker. Output in fact grew much faster than employment.

options.text: The American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886, organized skilled craft workers to bargain for higher wages and shorter hours
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The AFL's founding is accurate, but union demands for better pay do not show that employers lowered labor costs.

options.text: The Knights of Labor won a federal eight-hour law for industrial workers after the Haymarket affair of 1886 in Chicago
options.label: reversal
options.why: Haymarket hurt the Knights, and no federal eight-hour law for industrial workers passed. Such a law would also cut against the argument.

derived.desc: Ratio of workers employed, 1895 to 1870

items.stem: The change in the foreign-born share of workers shown in the table is best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: From the 1880s onward, a growing share of immigrants to the United States came from southern and eastern Europe.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred most Chinese laborers from entering the United States.
Irish immigration peaked after the famine of the late 1840s.

options.text: Rising immigration from southern and eastern Europe as industrial jobs drew new arrivals
options.label: key
options.why: The foreign-born share rose from 38 to 68 percent as the New Immigration from southern and eastern Europe supplied workers for expanding mills.

options.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which redirected Chinese laborers from western railroads into eastern steel mills
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 1882 act barred most Chinese laborers from entering the country; it did not send Chinese workers into eastern mills.

options.text: The flight of Irish and German immigrants from famine and revolution in Europe that peaked in the late 1840s and early 1850s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That wave peaked decades before the 1870-1895 rise shown in the table.

options.text: The Great Migration of African Americans from the rural South to northern factories during and after the First World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration began in the 1910s, and it involved native-born Americans, so it cannot explain a rising foreign-born share.

derived.desc: Change in foreign-born share, 1870 to 1895 (percentage points)

items.stem: The pattern of rising output and falling prices in the table is most similar to which development in another industry during the period 1865-1898?
facts: By about 1880, John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil controlled roughly 90 percent of United States oil refining.
Standard Oil's efficiencies and consolidation lowered the price of kerosene in the late 1800s.
Granger laws of the 1870s set state maximum rates for railroads and grain elevators.

options.text: Standard Oil's consolidation of refining, which cut kerosene prices while absorbing rival firms
options.label: key
options.why: Like the steel works, Standard Oil pushed output up and prices down by cutting costs and consolidating, folding in competitors through horizontal integration.

options.text: The 1901 gusher at Spindletop in Texas, which flooded the market with crude oil and ended Pennsylvania's dominance
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Spindletop came in 1901, outside the period named in the stem, and it reflects a new oil discovery rather than lower production costs.

options.text: The Granger laws of the 1870s, in which midwestern states set maximum rates that railroads could charge for hauling grain
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Granger laws lowered prices by government order, not by industrial efficiency and higher output.

options.text: The rise of mail-order catalog firms that let rural families buy factory goods without paying markups to local merchants
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Mail-order retail changed how goods were distributed, but it does not match the pattern of a manufacturing industry raising output and cutting its own production costs.

input.title: Bound Labor in a Tidewater Virginia County, 1665-1719

sources.title: Bound Laborers Listed in Probate Inventories, Halloway County, Virginia, 1665-1719
sources.attribution: Compiled from estate inventories filed at the fictional Halloway County courthouse, Tidewater Virginia; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a data appendix to a colonial social history study)
sources.body: The table counts the indentured European servants and enslaved Africans named in planters' estate inventories during six five-year periods, with enslaved people as a percentage of all bound laborers listed.

columns: Enslaved Africans as percent of all bound laborers

items.stem: The change in the composition of bound labor shown in the table after the 1670s is best explained by which of the following?
facts: Bacon's Rebellion (1676) in Virginia drew support from frontier settlers, landless freedmen, and servants.
In the decades after 1676, Chesapeake planters increasingly replaced indentured servants with enslaved Africans, as fewer English laborers migrated.

options.text: Planters wary of landless former servants after the 1676 uprising increasingly bought enslaved Africans instead
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows the enslaved share jumping from 23.6 percent in 1675-1679 to 48.1 percent a decade later. After Bacon's Rebellion showed the danger of armed, landless freedmen, and as fewer English servants arrived, planters turned to enslaved Africans held for life.

options.text: Parliament's Navigation Acts barred English ship captains from carrying indentured servants to the tobacco-growing colonies of the Chesapeake
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Navigation Acts regulated where colonial goods could be shipped and which ships could carry them. They did not ban the servant trade, which went on into the 1700s.

options.text: Revival preachers of the Great Awakening persuaded many indentured servants to break their contracts and move to New England towns
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Awakening came in the 1730s and 1740s, well after the shift shown in the table, and it did not cause servants to leave Virginia in large numbers.

options.text: A shift from tobacco to wheat cultivation reduced planters' overall need for field laborers in the Chesapeake region
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Chesapeake's partial move to wheat came later in the 1700s. The table shows the total number of bound laborers rising, not falling, because tobacco planting was expanding.

items.stem: A historian argues that colonial law reinforced the trend in the table by making the status of enslaved Africans more permanent. Which evidence would best support this argument?
facts: A 1662 Virginia law declared that a child's status as free or enslaved followed the condition of the mother.
The Maryland Toleration Act (1649) protected the worship of Christians in Maryland.

options.text: A 1662 Virginia statute providing that children of enslaved mothers would also be enslaved
options.label: key
options.why: Making slavery hereditary through the mother turned it into a permanent status passed down through generations. That gave planters a strong reason to invest in enslaved laborers rather than servants with fixed terms, which supports the historian's argument.

options.text: The Navigation Acts of the 1650s and 1660s requiring that colonial tobacco be shipped only to English ports
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These laws are real, but they governed trade, not the legal status of laborers, so they do not show law making slavery permanent.

options.text: The Maryland Toleration Act of 1649, which protected the worship of Christians, both Protestant and Catholic, in that colony
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Toleration Act dealt with religious freedom among Christians and had nothing to do with defining slavery or labor.

options.text: The creation of the House of Burgesses in 1619, which gave Virginia's landholding planters a voice in levying colonial taxes
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The House of Burgesses later passed slave laws, but the fact that it was founded says nothing about slavery becoming a permanent legal status.

items.stem: The trend shown in the table is best understood in the context of which broader development of the late 1600s and early 1700s?
facts: By the late 1600s and early 1700s, an Atlantic trade system linked colonial staple crops such as tobacco, British manufactured goods, and the transatlantic slave trade.
Most enslaved Africans brought to the British mainland colonies before 1750 went to the Chesapeake and the Carolina Lowcountry.

options.text: The growth of an Atlantic trade linking colonial staple crops, British manufactures, and the African slave trade
options.label: key
options.why: The rising number of enslaved people in a tobacco county shows how the Chesapeake was being drawn into an expanding Atlantic economy. Tobacco went to Britain, and the slave trade brought more and more Africans to the colonies.

options.text: The spread of Enlightenment ideas about natural rights that led colonial assemblies to restrict the importation of enslaved people
options.label: reversal
options.why: Revolutionary-era limits on the slave trade came after the 1760s. The table shows slave imports growing, not shrinking.

options.text: The expansion of French fur-trading networks and alliances with American Indian nations throughout the Great Lakes and Mississippi valleys
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: French fur-trade alliances were real in this period, but they did not shape labor patterns in Tidewater Virginia.

options.text: The Spanish effort to reassert control over New Mexico after the Pueblo Revolt by granting Pueblo communities more autonomy
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Spain did make some accommodations after reconquering New Mexico in the 1690s, but that development in the Southwest does not explain Chesapeake planters' turn to enslaved labor.

items.stem: The labor pattern in the table differed most from that of New England colonies in the same period in that New England
facts: Colonial New England's economy rested mainly on family farms, trade, and shipbuilding, with labor supplied largely by family members and hired hands.
Slavery was legal in New England in the 1600s and 1700s but on a much smaller scale, concentrated in ports and households.

options.text: relied mostly on family and hired labor, though slavery existed on a smaller scale in towns and households
options.label: key
options.why: New England's mixed economy of small farms, trade, and shipbuilding depended mostly on family members and wage labor. Slavery was legal there but limited, unlike the heavy reliance on enslaved labor shown in the Virginia table.

options.text: outlawed slavery entirely through Puritan legislatures and returned enslaved people who arrived on its ships to Africa
options.label: overstated
options.why: Slavery was legal in every New England colony during this period, and New England merchants took part in the slave trade.

options.text: used enslaved Africans primarily on large rice and indigo plantations in the coastal lowlands, as Carolina planters did
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Rice and indigo plantations belonged to the Carolina Lowcountry, not to New England.

options.text: drew most of its agricultural labor from American Indians compelled to work through an encomienda system modeled on Spain's
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The encomienda was a Spanish colonial institution. New England did not run on a coerced Native labor system of that kind.

input.title: Jobs in the Information Economy: Larkspur County, 1980-2000

sources.title: Employment by Selected Sector, Larkspur County, 1980, 1990, and 2000 (thousands of jobs)
sources.attribution: Larkspur County Economic Development Board, a fictional county agency, annual report presented to the county council, 2001; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a county economic development report)
sources.body: A table showing employment, in thousands of jobs, in five sectors of a fictional metropolitan county in 1980, 1990, and 2000.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly explains the growth in computer and software services employment in the county between 1990 and 2000, as shown in the table?
facts: The World Wide Web became publicly available in the early 1990s, and commercial internet use expanded rapidly by the mid-1990s.
The North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in 1994 and was associated with the movement of some manufacturing jobs from the United States to Mexico.

options.text: Expanding business and household use of personal computers and the internet attracted heavy investment in technology firms.
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows computer and software jobs rising from 15 to 48 thousand in the 1990s, the decade when personal computers and the commercial internet spread widely and investors poured money into technology companies.

options.text: Federal deregulation of the airline and trucking industries in the late 1970s lowered transportation costs for firms nationwide.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Transportation deregulation was real but came earlier and does not explain a surge specifically in computer and software employment.

options.text: Defense spending on the Strategic Defense Initiative under Reagan created permanent civilian demand for software programmers in the 1990s.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Defense research did support computing, but SDI was a 1980s military program and did not create the commercial, consumer-driven software boom of the 1990s.

options.text: Tariff reductions under the North American Free Trade Agreement encouraged firms to relocate data-processing jobs from Mexico into the United States.
options.label: reversal
options.why: NAFTA was associated with jobs moving from the United States to Mexico, mostly in manufacturing, not with jobs moving into the United States.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?

derived.desc: Manufacturing jobs lost 1980-2000
Telecommunications jobs gained 1980-2000
Computer services growth 1980-1990
Computer services growth 1990-2000

facts: In the 1980s and 1990s, manufacturing's share of U.S. employment declined while service-sector and information-related employment grew.

options.text: Service and information jobs grew while manufacturing employment in the county fell between 1980 and 2000.
options.label: key
options.why: Manufacturing fell from 96 to 52 thousand while every service and information sector listed grew, matching the national shift toward a service and information economy.

options.text: Computer and software services had become the county's largest source of jobs by 2000, surpassing retail trade employment.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: In 2000 computer services had 48 thousand jobs, still well below retail trade at 74 thousand.

options.text: New telecommunications jobs created between 1980 and 2000 fully replaced the manufacturing jobs the county lost in those years.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Telecommunications added only 10 thousand jobs while manufacturing lost 44 thousand.

options.text: Most growth in computer and software services occurred during the 1980s, before the internet came into wide commercial use.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sector grew by 11 thousand in the 1980s but by 33 thousand in the 1990s, so most growth came in the internet decade.

items.stem: The change in durable goods manufacturing employment shown in the table is best understood in the context of which broader development?
facts: From the 1970s onward, deindustrialization in the United States cost many manufacturing jobs as firms faced foreign competition and moved production to lower-wage regions and abroad.
Private-sector labor union membership in the United States declined steadily from the 1970s through the 2000s.

options.text: Deindustrialization as firms moved production to lower-wage regions and overseas amid rising global competition
options.label: key
options.why: The steady fall in manufacturing jobs from 1980 to 2000 fits the long trend of deindustrialization driven by globalization, foreign competition, and relocation of production.

options.text: The postwar migration of factories and workers from northern cities to the Sun Belt that peaked during the early 1950s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Sun Belt growth was real but continued over many decades, and a 1950s framing does not explain job losses from 1980 to 2000.

options.text: The rapid growth of private-sector labor union membership, which raised wages and forced many factories to close their doors
options.label: reversal
options.why: Private-sector union membership was shrinking, not growing, in the 1980s and 1990s.

options.text: The end of the Cold War, which eliminated nearly all federal defense contracts and shut down every type of manufacturing
options.label: overstated
options.why: Defense cuts after 1991 hurt some industries, but they did not eliminate defense contracting or account for the general decline in manufacturing.

items.stem: The trend in computer and software services employment shown in the table was most directly connected to which development at the end of the 1990s?
facts: Speculation in internet stocks in the late 1990s ended in the dot-com crash, as technology stock prices fell sharply beginning in 2000.
The federal government ran budget surpluses from 1998 through 2001.

options.text: A surge of speculative investment in internet companies that ended with a sharp fall in technology stock prices in 2000
options.label: key
options.why: The rapid technology job growth of the 1990s was tied to heavy investment in internet firms, a bubble that burst in the dot-com crash starting in 2000.

options.text: A wave of risky subprime home lending that collapsed into a financial crisis and severe recession beginning in 2007 and 2008
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The subprime crisis came nearly a decade later and grew out of housing finance, not the 1990s technology boom.

options.text: Federal budget deficits that grew larger every year of the late 1990s as tax revenues from a weakening economy declined
options.label: reversal
options.why: A strong economy raised tax revenues in the late 1990s, and the federal government ran surpluses from 1998 to 2001.

options.text: Persistent stagflation, combining high inflation with high unemployment, like the conditions that troubled the economy in the 1970s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The late 1990s had low inflation and low unemployment; stagflation describes the 1970s economy.

input.title: The Compromise of 1877 and the Making of Sharecropping

sources.title: Settlement Tables and Statehouses
sources.attribution: Delphine Arceneaux, historian, Settling Accounts: Land, Credit, and the Retreat from Reconstruction in the Cotton South, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian of Reconstruction)
sources.body: Historians often treat the bargain that settled the disputed election of 1876 as the moment Reconstruction ended. In the cotton districts of Georgia and the Carolinas, however, the decisive retreat had begun years earlier, at the settlement table rather than the ballot box. Freedpeople had hoped for land of their own. When federal authorities returned confiscated and abandoned plantations to their former owners in 1865 and 1866, most freedpeople were left to bargain for shares of a crop they could not market themselves. By the early 1870s, lien laws passed by Southern legislatures gave merchants a first claim on the harvest, and tenants who ended the year in debt found themselves bound to the same landlord for another season. The withdrawal of federal troops from Southern statehouses in 1877 did not create this system. It removed the last outside authority to which Black farmers could appeal when contracts were broken, and it handed enforcement to Redeemer governments with every reason to tighten the terms.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's argument that the decisive retreat from Reconstruction began well before 1877?

options.text: Congress in the late 1860s declined to adopt proposals to divide confiscated planter estates among freedpeople.
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues that the retreat began over land and labor in the 1860s. Congress's refusal to adopt land redistribution proposals, such as those Radical Republicans pushed in 1867, left freedpeople without land and is evidence of an early retreat.

options.text: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, barred states from denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous servitude.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Fifteenth Amendment widened federal protection of Black rights. It shows Reconstruction expanding in this period, so it does not show an early retreat.

options.text: Freedmen's Bureau teachers and Northern missionary societies founded hundreds of schools for formerly enslaved children and adults across the South.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The school-building is real, but it is an achievement of Reconstruction. It says nothing about land, credit, or an early retreat.

options.text: Thousands of Black Southerners left Louisiana and Mississippi to settle in Kansas during the Exoduster migration of 1879.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Exoduster migration came after 1877. It cannot show that the retreat began before the Compromise.

facts: Proposals by Radical Republicans such as Thaddeus Stevens in 1867 to confiscate and redistribute planter land to freedpeople were not enacted by Congress.
President Andrew Johnson's pardons led to most confiscated and abandoned Southern land being returned to former owners in 1865-1866.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly modify the author's claim that the withdrawal of federal troops in 1877 removed the last outside authority to which Black farmers could appeal?

options.text: Congress had shut down nearly all Freedmen's Bureau operations, including its handling of labor disputes, by 1872.
options.label: key
options.why: The Freedmen's Bureau had settled contract disputes between freedpeople and planters. Because Congress closed it by 1872, the main federal channel for labor complaints was gone before 1877, which complicates the author's claim about what 1877 removed.

options.text: Redeemer legislatures after 1877 strengthened lien and vagrancy laws that tied tenants and laborers more tightly to landlords.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This fits the author's claim that Redeemer governments tightened the terms after 1877. It supports the argument rather than modifying it.

options.text: Rutherford B. Hayes became president after an electoral commission awarded him all twenty disputed electoral votes in 1877.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is an accurate account of how the disputed election was settled. It says nothing about whether any federal authority still protected Black farmers' contracts.

options.text: Congress passed the Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871 to let federal authorities prosecute Klan violence against voters.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Enforcement Acts show that federal authority was active before 1877. That is consistent with the author's view that federal power was the outside check that later disappeared.

facts: Congress ended the Freedmen's Bureau in 1872, and most of its functions had stopped by 1869.
Through its agents, the Freedmen's Bureau supervised labor contracts between freedpeople and planters.

items.stem: The bargain over the disputed election of 1876 mentioned in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: Northern voters' waning commitment to Reconstruction amid the economic depression that followed the Panic of 1873
options.label: key
options.why: After the Panic of 1873 and a series of Grant-era scandals, Northern voters and Republicans turned toward economic concerns and grew tired of enforcing Reconstruction. That made a deal ending federal intervention in Southern politics acceptable in 1877.

options.text: Sectional disputes over whether slavery would be permitted in the vast territories acquired from Mexico in 1848
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The fight over slavery in the Mexican Cession belongs to the late 1840s and 1850s. The Thirteenth Amendment had ended slavery by 1876.

options.text: Radical Republicans' efforts to remove President Andrew Johnson from office after he obstructed congressional plans for the South
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Johnson's impeachment came in 1868, during the expansion of congressional Reconstruction, not during its collapse.

options.text: Populist demands for free coinage of silver, government ownership of railroads, and a graduated federal income tax
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The People's Party made these demands in the 1890s, long after the 1877 settlement.

facts: The Panic of 1873 began a severe economic depression that shifted Northern political attention away from Reconstruction.
In the Compromise of 1877, Rutherford B. Hayes became president and federal troops were withdrawn from Southern statehouses in South Carolina and Louisiana.

items.stem: The credit and labor arrangements described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the late nineteenth century?

options.text: Southern Farmers' Alliances promoting cooperatives and a subtreasury plan to free growers from merchant credit
options.label: key
options.why: Crop liens and debt peonage kept Southern farmers dependent on furnishing merchants. In the 1880s and 1890s, Southern Farmers' Alliances answered with cooperative stores and the subtreasury plan, which would have given farmers low-cost federal credit against stored crops.

options.text: Midwestern Grangers persuading state legislatures to pass laws regulating the rates charged by railroads and grain elevators
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Granger laws were a real farmer protest, but they grew out of Midwestern complaints about railroad and elevator rates, not Southern crop liens and sharecropping.

options.text: The Knights of Labor organizing skilled and unskilled industrial workers in a national campaign for an eight-hour workday
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Knights' eight-hour campaign responded to industrial wage labor, not to Southern agricultural tenancy and crop-lien debt.

options.text: Congress passing the Dawes Act to divide reservation lands into individual allotments for Native American families
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Dawes Act of 1887 grew out of federal Indian policy. It had nothing to do with Southern credit or tenancy.

facts: Southern Farmers' Alliances in the 1880s organized cooperatives, and in 1889-1890 they proposed the subtreasury plan to give farmers credit against stored crops.
Crop-lien systems in the postwar South tied tenants and sharecroppers to merchants and landlords through debt.

input.title: An Independent Mill Owner Testifies Against the Trusts, 1889

sources.title: Testimony of a linseed oil mill owner before a state legislative committee investigating trusts, 1889
sources.attribution: Testimony of Josiah Merrow, owner of a linseed oil mill in the fictional town of Harlan Falls, Ohio, given before a committee of the Ohio legislature investigating business combinations, 1889 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Gilded Age legislative testimony)
sources.body: Gentlemen of the committee, I have pressed linseed oil at Harlan Falls for nineteen years, and I employ thirty-one men. Two years ago agents of the new oil combination offered me trust certificates in exchange for my mill. When I refused, the price of oil in my territory fell below what it costs me to buy the flaxseed. The railroad that carries my barrels to Cleveland now charges me nearly double what it charges the combination, which collects a rebate on every car it ships. My neighbors in this trade have sold out one by one. Their mills stand idle, and a board of trustees in New York decides how much oil the country shall have and at what price. I do not ask for favors. I ask that the law forbid any contract or combination meant to destroy competition, and since these trusts reach across every state line, that Congress act where Ohio alone cannot.

items.stem: The author's main purpose in giving this testimony was most likely to

options.text: persuade lawmakers to outlaw combinations that crushed small competitors through rebates and price cutting
options.label: key
options.why: Merrow describes predatory pricing and railroad rebates that favored the combination, then asks that the law forbid combinations meant to destroy competition, the same concerns that produced state antitrust laws and the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

options.text: win support for federal ownership of the railroads and telegraphs, a demand later adopted in the Populist Omaha Platform of 1892
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Merrow complains about discriminatory rates but asks only for a ban on anticompetitive combinations, not government ownership; the Omaha Platform demand came later and from a different movement.

options.text: convince legislators to raise protective tariffs so that domestic oil mills could compete against cheaper imported products from Europe
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The threat Merrow describes comes from a domestic trust and railroad favoritism, not from foreign imports; tariffs are never mentioned.

options.text: build public support for the Knights of Labor's campaign for an eight-hour workday among the mill hands he employed
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Knights of Labor did push for the eight-hour day in the 1880s, but Merrow speaks as an owner about competition, not as an advocate for workers' hours.

facts: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 declared illegal every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy in restraint of trade among the states.
Railroad rebates to large shippers were a major complaint of independent producers in the 1870s and 1880s.

items.stem: Which of the following would best support the author's claim that Congress, rather than individual states, needed to act against the trusts?

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in Wabash v. Illinois (1886) that states could not regulate interstate railroad rates
options.label: key
options.why: Wabash limited state power over commerce that crossed state lines, supporting Merrow's point that Ohio alone could not control combinations and railroads operating across many states.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in Munn v. Illinois (1877) upholding a state law that set maximum rates for grain elevators
options.label: reversal
options.why: Munn affirmed state power to regulate businesses affecting the public interest, which would weaken rather than support the claim that states could not act.

options.text: The passage of the Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883), which required competitive examinations for many federal government positions
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Pendleton Act addressed the spoils system in federal hiring, not the limits of state power over interstate business.

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) that narrowly interpreted the privileges protected by the Fourteenth Amendment
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Slaughterhouse Cases limited federal protection of citizens' rights under the Fourteenth Amendment; they say nothing about states' inability to regulate interstate combinations.

facts: In Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific Railway Co. v. Illinois (1886), the Supreme Court ruled that states could not regulate interstate railroad rates.
In Munn v. Illinois (1877), the Supreme Court upheld an Illinois law regulating grain elevator rates.

items.stem: The situation the author describes is best understood in the context of which broader development of the late nineteenth century?

options.text: The consolidation of industries by large firms that absorbed or ruined smaller competitors
options.label: key
options.why: The combination offering trust certificates and driving out rival mills is an example of horizontal integration and the trust form that business leaders used to consolidate industries such as oil refining in the 1870s and 1880s.

options.text: The movement of textile and tobacco manufacturing into the South as boosters promoted a New South built on cheap labor
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: New South industrialization did happen, but the excerpt is about an Ohio mill being squeezed by a national combination, not regional industrial growth.

options.text: The growth of craft unions such as the American Federation of Labor, which bargained for higher wages for skilled workers
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The AFL was founded in 1886, but the excerpt is about competition between businesses, not organized labor.

options.text: The federal government's grants of land and loans to railroad companies to speed construction of the transcontinental lines
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Federal railroad subsidies were real, but Merrow's complaint is about rebates and the trust's pricing, not how the railroads were financed.

facts: In the late nineteenth century, firms such as Standard Oil used horizontal integration and the trust device to consolidate their industries.
Trust certificates were exchanged for stock in companies brought under a trust's control in the 1880s.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, passed amid complaints like the author's, related to later developments?

options.text: Its weak early enforcement led Progressive Era reformers to seek stronger laws such as the Clayton Act of 1914
options.label: key
options.why: Vague wording and court rulings such as United States v. E. C. Knight (1895) limited the Sherman Act, so Progressives pressed for the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Federal Trade Commission in 1914.

options.text: It broke up most of the large trusts within a few years and brought the wave of corporate mergers to an end before 1900
options.label: reversal
options.why: The act was rarely and weakly enforced in the 1890s, and a major merger wave actually took place around 1895 to 1904.

options.text: It created the Interstate Commerce Commission, which later gained power under Theodore Roosevelt to set maximum railroad rates
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The ICC was created by the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, not the Sherman Act, though the Hepburn Act of 1906 later strengthened it.

options.text: It led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve System in 1913 to keep trusts from controlling the nation's supply of credit
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 came out of banking and currency reform after the Panic of 1907, not out of the Sherman Act.

facts: In United States v. E. C. Knight Co. (1895), the Supreme Court ruled that the Sherman Act did not apply to manufacturing, which weakened its enforcement.
The Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914 strengthened federal antitrust law during the Progressive Era.
The Interstate Commerce Commission was created by the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.

input.title: Explaining Medicare to a Senior Citizens' Club, 1966

sources.title: Address on the new Medicare program
sources.attribution: Speech by Edna Forsythe Marlowe, administrator of Pell County Memorial Hospital, to the Golden Age Club of a small Iowa town, May 1966 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a community address by a rural hospital administrator)
sources.body: Friends, on the first of July this hospital will begin honoring the new Medicare card, and I want every one of you to sign up for the doctor's insurance before the enrollment period closes. For a few dollars a month, the government will share the cost of your physician's bills. The hospital insurance comes to you without any premium at all, because you paid for it through your Social Security taxes over a lifetime of work. Last winter I watched a retired railroad man sell his house to pay for six weeks in our ward. That should not happen in the richest nation on earth. Some of you have read that the doctors' association calls this socialized medicine. I can only tell you that no clerk in Washington will choose your doctor for you. And for neighbors too poor to pay even the small share, the state is preparing its own program under the same law.

items.stem: The primary purpose of Marlowe's speech was most likely
facts: Medicare was signed into law in July 1965 as an amendment to the Social Security Act and began providing benefits on July 1, 1966.
The American Medical Association opposed Medicare, often describing government health insurance as socialized medicine.

options.text: to persuade older listeners to enroll in a newly enacted federal program and to answer critics' objections to it
options.label: key
options.why: Marlowe urges seniors to sign up before enrollment closes and rebuts the socialized medicine charge, reflecting Medicare's 1966 launch after its 1965 passage.

options.text: to pressure members of Congress into passing a compulsory national health insurance plan that would cover Americans of every age
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The speech treats Medicare as already law and addresses seniors, not Congress; universal coverage for all ages is never proposed.

options.text: to warn elderly patients that federal control of hospitals would soon limit their freedom to choose their own physicians
options.label: reversal
options.why: Marlowe explicitly rejects the claim that Washington will choose patients' doctors; this reverses her point of view.

options.text: to win support from local taxpayers for a county bond issue to build new hospital wards for the growing number of retirees
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Nothing in the speech concerns local construction financing; its focus is enrollment in federal insurance.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support Marlowe's argument that older Americans needed the new program?
facts: Before Medicare, private health insurance in the United States was largely tied to employment, and many Americans over sixty-five lacked hospital insurance.
In the 1950s, Congress extended Social Security coverage to many farm and domestic workers and to self-employed people.

options.text: Before 1965, many Americans over sixty-five lacked hospital insurance because private plans were tied to jobs or cost too much
options.label: key
options.why: Widespread lack of coverage among retirees directly supports the claim, illustrated by the railroad man who sold his house, that seniors faced ruinous medical bills.

options.text: The American Medical Association spent heavily in the early 1960s on advertising and lobbying campaigns against government health insurance for retirees
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This explains the opposition Marlowe mentions but offers no evidence that seniors actually needed coverage.

options.text: Rising median family incomes in the 1950s allowed millions of working households to buy homes in new suburban developments
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Postwar prosperity among working families says nothing about retirees' medical costs and does not support her argument.

options.text: In the 1950s, Congress extended Social Security old-age pensions to farm workers, domestic workers, and the self-employed
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Broader pension coverage is real but concerns retirement income, not the specific problem of uninsured medical expenses.

items.stem: Marlowe's speech was most likely delivered in the context of
facts: Medicare and Medicaid were part of President Lyndon Johnson's Great Society, enacted in 1965.
President Harry Truman proposed national health insurance in the late 1940s, but Congress did not enact it.

options.text: an expansion of federal social programs aimed at reducing poverty under President Lyndon Johnson
options.label: key
options.why: Medicare was one of the Great Society laws of 1965, alongside War on Poverty measures that greatly expanded the federal role in social welfare.

options.text: the enactment of President Harry Truman's Fair Deal proposal for a system of national health insurance funded through payroll taxes
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Truman's national health insurance proposal failed in Congress; Medicare came under Johnson in 1965.

options.text: a congressional effort to reduce federal spending on social welfare and shift responsibility for poverty programs to the states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Efforts to cut and devolve welfare spending marked the 1980s conservative era, not the mid-1960s expansion.

options.text: the creation of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance under the Social Security Act during the Great Depression
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Social Security Act of 1935 is background for Medicare's financing, but the speech belongs to the 1960s, three decades later.

items.stem: The state program Marlowe mentions at the end of the excerpt refers to which of the following?
facts: Medicaid, created by the 1965 Social Security Amendments, is a joint federal-state program that pays medical costs for low-income people.
Head Start and the Job Corps were War on Poverty programs established in the mid-1960s.

options.text: Medicaid, which combined federal and state funds to pay medical costs for low-income people
options.label: key
options.why: Medicaid was created by the same 1965 law as Medicare and run by the states with federal matching funds for the poor.

options.text: Aid to Dependent Children, a New Deal program that gave cash assistance to poor families with children
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: ADC dated from 1935 and provided cash aid, not a new medical program created under the 1965 law.

options.text: Head Start, a War on Poverty program that funded preschool education, meals, and health screenings for poor children
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Head Start was a Great Society program, but it focused on early childhood education, not medical bills for poor adults.

options.text: the Job Corps, which provided vocational training and residential education for unemployed young people under the Economic Opportunity Act
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Job Corps was a War on Poverty job-training program, unrelated to paying medical costs.

input.title: Boom and Enclosure at a Kansas Cattle Railhead, 1870-1890

sources.title: Cattle Trade and Fencing at Sedgewater Junction, Kansas, Selected Years, 1870-1890
sources.attribution: Summary prepared for the Sedgewater Junction Stock Yards Company and the Pawnee Fork County assessor, 1891; fictional railhead town and county; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age stockyard annual report)
sources.body: The table shows Texas cattle arriving by trail drive, cattle shipped east by rail, average prices paid per head at the railhead, and miles of barbed-wire fence recorded in the surrounding county for selected years.

columns: Texas cattle received by trail drive (thousands of head)
Cattle shipped east by rail, trail and local ranch herds (thousands of head)
Average price per head at railhead (dollars)

items.stem: The trends in the table between 1870 and 1882 best illustrate which of the following developments?
facts: After the Civil War, Texas cattle were driven north to Kansas railheads such as Abilene (opened 1867) for shipment to eastern markets.
Railroads and Chicago meatpacking, aided by refrigerated rail cars by the late 1870s and 1880s, supplied beef to growing eastern cities.

options.text: The rise of a range cattle industry that relied on railroads to supply beef to growing eastern cities
options.label: key
options.why: Trail receipts, rail shipments, and prices all climb to 1882, showing the long drive feeding railheads that moved beef to urban markets, the core of the post-Civil War cattle boom.

options.text: The spread of subsistence homesteading in which Plains families raised small herds chiefly for their own household consumption
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table shows tens of thousands of head shipped east for sale, a commercial market trade, not subsistence production.

options.text: The expansion of federal reservation policy that guaranteed Plains nations control over the grasslands crossed by the trail drives
options.label: reversal
options.why: Federal policy in this period shrank Native land holdings and opened the Plains to ranchers, rather than guaranteeing Native control of the grasslands.

options.text: The success of Grange cooperatives that let small Texas ranchers bypass the railroads and ship their own cattle directly to Chicago
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Grange mainly organized farmers against railroad rates and pushed for regulation; it did not let ranchers get around the railroads, which carried the cattle shown in the table.

items.stem: Which data from the table would best support the argument that the closing of the open range reshaped the county's cattle business after 1882?
facts: Joseph Glidden patented a successful barbed wire in 1874, and its cheap mass production allowed ranchers and farmers to fence the Plains.
By the late 1880s, fencing and quarantine laws against Texas fever largely ended the long cattle drives to Kansas.

options.text: Trail receipts fell to zero by 1890 as fence mileage rose from 60 to 340
options.label: key
options.why: The trail drives disappeared while barbed wire spread 280 miles after 1882, which directly links enclosure to the end of open-range droving.

options.text: The average price per head rose from 20 dollars in 1878 to 32 dollars in 1882, the highest figure shown
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it describes the boom before 1882 and says nothing about fencing or the closing of the range afterward.

options.text: Trail receipts more than doubled from 40,000 head in 1870 to 95,000 head in 1874 as railheads opened
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This growth came during the early open-range expansion, not the post-1882 change the argument is about.

options.text: Rail shipments in 1890 remained about three times as large as they had been in 1870, showing continuing demand
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Continuing rail shipments point to steady demand. They do not show the range being enclosed or the trail trade collapsing.

derived.desc: Increase in miles of barbed-wire fence, 1882 to 1890
Ratio of rail shipments 1890 to 1870 (thousands of head)

items.stem: The drop in trail cattle received and in prices between 1882 and 1887 shown in the table most directly reflected which of the following?
facts: Overstocking of the Plains ranges in the early 1880s drove cattle prices down after about 1882.
The severe winter of 1886-1887 killed huge numbers of range cattle and ruined many ranching companies.

options.text: Overstocked ranges and the severe winter of 1886 to 1887, which killed large numbers of cattle
options.label: key
options.why: Speculative overstocking pushed prices down after 1882, and the disastrous winter of 1886-1887 wiped out herds. This matches the falling prices and receipts by 1887.

options.text: The Panic of 1893, which bankrupted railroads and cut off eastern credit to western ranching companies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Panic of 1893 came after every year shown in the table, so it cannot explain changes between 1882 and 1887.

options.text: The Dawes Act, which opened former reservation grazing lands and flooded the market with Native-owned cattle herds
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Dawes Act (1887) split reservation land into individual allotments. It did not create a flood of Native-owned cattle, and it came too late to cause the decline after 1882.

options.text: The Interstate Commerce Act, which forced railroads to stop carrying Texas cattle across state lines to Kansas
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1887 act regulated railroad rates and banned practices such as rebates; it did not prohibit the shipment of cattle.

items.stem: The county's shift from trail herds on open range to fenced ranches most closely parallels which development in western mining between 1865 and 1898?
facts: In western mining districts such as the Comstock Lode in Nevada, individual placer prospecting gave way to corporate hard-rock mining that required heavy capital investment.
The Sherman Silver Purchase Act (1890) required the federal Treasury to buy silver; it did not give the government ownership of mines.

options.text: Individual placer prospectors giving way to corporate hard-rock mining backed by eastern capital
options.label: key
options.why: Like ranching, which moved from open-range drives to fenced, heavily capitalized operations, mining moved from lone prospectors to large corporations after easy surface deposits ran out.

options.text: The rush of independent forty-niners to the California goldfields following the discovery at Sutter's Mill
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The California Gold Rush came after the 1848 discovery, well before 1865. It was also an early rush, not a later consolidation.

options.text: Large mining corporations selling their deep shafts to cooperatives owned and managed by the miners themselves
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ownership in western mining became more concentrated in corporations; it did not pass to worker cooperatives.

options.text: The federal government taking ownership of western silver mines after passage of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1890 act required the Treasury to buy silver, and the mines stayed in private hands.

input.title: A Baltimore Ship Owner Responds to the Monroe Doctrine, 1824

sources.title: Letter to the editor on the President's annual message
sources.attribution: Elias Tolland, a ship owner of Fells Point, Baltimore, letter to the editor of the Baltimore Mercantile Register, January 1824 (fictional author and newspaper) (ALTON-composed, in the style of an early nineteenth-century merchant's newspaper letter)
sources.body: Sir, my vessels have carried flour and cotton cloth to Buenos Aires, Valparaiso, and Cartagena these four years, and returned with hides, copper, and silver coin. Such commerce was impossible while Spain kept her colonies shut to every flag but her own. I therefore read the President's late message with relief. The talk along our wharves is that the crowned heads who crushed the liberals of Spain mean next to lend their armies to restore King Ferdinand's rule across the ocean. Let them understand that this hemisphere is closed to new colonies, whether planted by Madrid or by the Czar on the northwest coast. Some gentlemen wished us to sign a joint pledge with London. I am glad we spoke alone, for we ought not to bind ourselves to any European court. I confess our little navy could not stop a great fleet. Yet the English want these markets as badly as we do, and their ships will keep the sea lanes open.

items.stem: The author's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: New trading opportunities created when Spain's American colonies won independence
options.label: key
options.why: The author describes trade with Buenos Aires, Valparaiso, and Cartagena that Spain's closed colonial system had blocked. The Latin American independence movements of the 1810s and early 1820s opened those markets to United States merchants.

options.text: The Embargo Act's ban on American exports, which ruined many Baltimore ship owners and merchants
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The embargo ran from 1807 to 1809. The author is concerned with protecting the Latin American trade he is carrying on in the 1820s, not with an earlier ban on exports.

options.text: Southern planters' fear that high protective tariffs on manufactured goods would provoke European retaliation
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The author is a Baltimore ship owner worried about European recolonization. Tariff disputes, which peaked with the Tariff of 1828, have no part in his argument.

options.text: The opening of the Erie Canal, which shifted western grain shipments toward the port of New York
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Erie Canal was finished in 1825 and concerned internal trade. The letter is about overseas commerce and European threats to the hemisphere.

facts: Most of Spain's mainland American colonies, including Argentina, Chile, and Gran Colombia, won independence between about 1810 and 1825.
The United States recognized several Latin American republics beginning in 1822.

items.stem: The author of the excerpt argues that the United States should

options.text: oppose European recolonization in the Americas while staying out of European alliances
options.label: key
options.why: The author says the hemisphere is closed to new colonies and approves of the United States speaking alone rather than binding itself to any European court. This matches the Monroe Doctrine's two principles: no further colonization, and no American involvement in European affairs.

options.text: join Great Britain in a formal treaty guaranteeing the independence of the Latin American republics
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author is glad the United States turned down a joint pledge with London. Secretary of State John Quincy Adams pushed for a unilateral statement instead of the joint declaration Britain proposed.

options.text: build a navy large enough to defeat any European fleet before declaring its opposition to colonization
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author admits the navy is small and relies on British self-interest to keep the sea lanes open. He does not call for a naval buildup.

options.text: send American troops to defend the new republics against any Spanish attempt at reconquest
options.label: overstated
options.why: The letter backs a declaration of principle, not military intervention. The Monroe Doctrine committed no troops to defend Latin America.

facts: President James Monroe announced the Monroe Doctrine in his annual message to Congress in December 1823.

Secretary of State John Quincy Adams persuaded Monroe to issue a unilateral statement rather than a joint declaration with Britain, which British Foreign Secretary George Canning had proposed in 1823.

items.stem: The concerns expressed in the excerpt are best understood in the context of

options.text: fears that European monarchies would help Spain reclaim its lost American colonies
options.label: key
options.why: The author mentions the crowned heads who crushed Spain's liberals. France, backed by the conservative European powers, invaded Spain in 1823 and restored Ferdinand VII, which raised fears of an expedition to retake Spain's former colonies. Russian claims on the northwest coast added to these worries.

options.text: British impressment of American sailors and seizure of cargoes during the Napoleonic Wars
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Impressment was a grievance before the War of 1812. In this letter Britain is a commercial partner whose navy helps the United States, not a threat to American shipping.

options.text: the undeclared naval war with France that followed the XYZ Affair and disrupted American shipping
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Quasi-War took place from 1798 to 1800. The letter answers the President's message of late 1823 and the European situation of the early 1820s.

options.text: disputes with Mexico over the annexation of Texas and the location of the Rio Grande boundary
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The quarrels over Texas annexation and the Rio Grande border came in the 1840s. In 1824 the author treats the new Spanish American republics as trading partners to protect.

facts: In 1823 a French army, acting with the approval of the conservative European powers, invaded Spain and restored King Ferdinand VII to full power.
A Russian imperial decree of 1821 claimed the Pacific coast down to the 51st parallel, which prompted American objections.

items.stem: The excerpt's view of relations with European powers most directly reflects continuity with which earlier development?

options.text: Washington's advice in his Farewell Address to avoid permanent foreign alliances
options.label: key
options.why: The author's insistence that the nation not bind itself to any European court carries on the principle in Washington's 1796 Farewell Address, which warned against permanent alliances with foreign powers.

options.text: The alliance with France in 1778 that brought French troops and ships to aid the Patriot cause
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 1778 treaty was a formal alliance with a European monarchy, which is exactly the kind of commitment the author rejects.

options.text: The Proclamation of 1763, which barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Proclamation was a British imperial policy on western settlement. It has no connection to the author's view of American alliances with Europe.

options.text: The Alien and Sedition Acts, which Federalists passed in 1798 to restrict pro-French critics
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These laws did come out of tensions with France, but they were domestic measures restricting immigrants and dissent. They were not a principle governing alliances with European powers.

facts: George Washington's Farewell Address, published in 1796, warned the United States against permanent alliances with foreign nations.
The United States signed a treaty of alliance with France in 1778 during the American Revolution.

input.title: Two Interpretations of Plessy v. Ferguson and the Rise of Jim Crow

sources.title: Excerpt A: Plessy as the End of a Long Retreat
sources.attribution: Leonard Castellano, historian, The Long Retreat: Federal Courts and the Unmaking of Reconstruction, 2004 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian of constitutional law)
sources.body: The decision in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 is best understood not as a turning point but as the last step in a long national retreat. By the time the justices approved Louisiana's Separate Car Act, the Court had already narrowed the Fourteenth Amendment in the Slaughterhouse Cases of 1873. In 1883 it had struck down the public accommodations sections of the Civil Rights Act of 1875. Northern voters and Republican leaders, tired of Southern questions and absorbed by tariffs and currency, had largely given up on enforcement after 1877. Plessy simply told white Southern lawmakers what they already knew: no branch of the federal government would stand in their way. The wave of segregation statutes after 1896 followed from that national consent.

sources.title: Excerpt B: Plessy as a Contested Test Case
sources.attribution: Adele Fontenot, historian, Citizens of the Crescent City: Black Activism and the Making of Plessy, 2015 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social historian of the Gulf South)
sources.body: Accounts that treat Plessy as a foregone conclusion overlook the people who brought it. In 1891 a group of Black and Creole of color professionals in New Orleans formed the Comite des Citoyens to challenge the state's 1890 law requiring separate railway cars. They raised money, hired the white attorney Albion Tourgee, and arranged for Homer Plessy, a shoemaker, to be arrested in 1892 for sitting in a car reserved for whites. Their aim was a national test of the Fourteenth Amendment. They lost, but the case shows that segregation was imposed over organized opposition, not accepted quietly. Jim Crow had to be built law by law because Black Southerners kept contesting it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the interpretations in the two excerpts?

options.text: Castellano stresses the federal government's abandonment of Reconstruction, while Fontenot stresses organized Black resistance to segregation.
options.label: key
options.why: Castellano explains Plessy as the result of court rulings and Northern loss of interest after 1877. Fontenot centers the Comite des Citoyens and argues that segregation was imposed over organized opposition.

options.text: Castellano argues that Plessy marked a sudden break from earlier federal policy, while Fontenot argues that the ruling merely confirmed long-standing Southern custom.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This flips the argument. Castellano says Plessy was the last step in a long retreat, not a break. Fontenot denies that segregation was quietly accepted custom.

options.text: Castellano blames Northern business interests for writing segregation laws, while Fontenot blames Southern Democratic legislators who were trying to win back Populist voters.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt makes these claims. Castellano says Northerners gave up on enforcement, not that they wrote the laws, and Fontenot never mentions Populists.

options.text: Both historians argue that the Supreme Court's ruling surprised contemporaries, who had widely expected the justices to strike down Louisiana's Separate Car Act.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Castellano says Southern lawmakers already expected federal non-interference. Fontenot says the activists lost but does not claim the outcome surprised people.

facts: The Supreme Court upheld Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), establishing the separate but equal doctrine.
In the Civil Rights Cases (1883) the Supreme Court struck down the public accommodations provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
The Comite des Citoyens of New Orleans organized Homer Plessy's 1892 test-case arrest.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Fontenot's argument in Excerpt B about how Jim Crow was established?

options.text: African Americans in many Southern cities organized boycotts of newly segregated streetcar lines in the early 1900s.
options.label: key
options.why: Organized boycotts against segregated streetcars show that Black Southerners kept contesting segregation as it spread. This directly supports Fontenot's claim that Jim Crow was imposed over opposition.

options.text: In an 1895 address in Atlanta, Booker T. Washington urged Black Southerners to put off agitation for social equality and focus on economic progress and vocational training.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Washington's accommodationist message would tend to complicate or challenge Fontenot's emphasis on steady resistance, not support it.
