options.text: In the Civil Rights Cases of 1883, the Supreme Court ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment did not reach discrimination by private businesses such as inns, theaters, and railroads.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it supports Castellano's argument about the judicial retreat rather than Fontenot's point about Black activism.

options.text: Mississippi's constitution of 1890 used poll taxes and literacy tests to remove most Black voters from the rolls without naming race directly in its provisions.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it shows white Southerners' methods of disfranchisement, not organized Black opposition to segregation.

facts: African Americans organized boycotts of segregated streetcars in many Southern cities between about 1900 and 1906.
Booker T. Washington delivered his Atlanta Exposition address, often called the Atlanta Compromise, in 1895.
Mississippi's 1890 constitution introduced poll taxes and literacy tests that disfranchised most Black voters.

items.stem: The spread of state segregation laws described in both excerpts took place most directly in the context of which of the following?

options.text: The return of white Democratic Redeemer governments to power across the former Confederacy
options.label: key
options.why: After Reconstruction ended, white Democrats calling themselves Redeemers regained control of Southern state governments. Those legislatures passed segregation laws such as Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act.

options.text: The expansion of federal protection of Black voting rights through the Enforcement Acts and the Ku Klux Klan Act
options.label: reversal
options.why: Those laws came in 1870 and 1871, and federal enforcement weakened afterward. Segregation spread because federal protection declined, not because it expanded.

options.text: The Great Migration of Black Southerners to Northern factory cities during and after the First World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Migration began in the 1910s, after the segregation laws of the 1890s were already in place.

options.text: The rapid growth of Black landownership made possible by federal redistribution of confiscated Confederate plantations
options.label: reversal
options.why: Large-scale land redistribution never happened. Most freedpeople ended up in sharecropping and tenancy, not landownership.

facts: By 1877 white Democratic Redeemer governments controlled all the former Confederate states.
Congress passed the Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871, but federal enforcement declined in the 1870s.
The Great Migration of African Americans to Northern cities began around the 1910s.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments was most directly a response to the legal order upheld in Plessy v. Ferguson?

options.text: The founding of the NAACP in 1909 to challenge segregation and disfranchisement in court
options.label: key
options.why: The NAACP, founded in 1909, set out to challenge the Jim Crow system that Plessy had legitimized, mainly through lawsuits. This continued the legal strategy of the Comite des Citoyens.

options.text: The passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1875, which banned racial discrimination in inns, theaters, and public conveyances
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Civil Rights Act of 1875 came two decades before Plessy, so it could not have been a response to it.

options.text: The ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, which barred states from denying citizens the vote on account of sex
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Nineteenth Amendment came out of the woman suffrage movement, not out of resistance to racial segregation.

options.text: The founding of the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama to train Black teachers and craftsmen in agricultural and industrial skills
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Tuskegee was founded in 1881, before Plessy, and it stressed vocational education rather than legal challenges to segregation.

facts: The NAACP was founded in 1909 and pursued legal challenges to segregation and disfranchisement.
The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, prohibited denial of the vote on account of sex.
The Tuskegee Institute was founded in Alabama in 1881.

input.title: Coaling Stations and Conscience: Interpreting the Territorial Gains of 1898

sources.title: A historian on the motives behind the territorial acquisitions of 1898
sources.attribution: Eleanor Vashti Corwin, Coaling Stations and Conscience: The Pacific Logic of 1898, a fictional diplomatic history, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic history monograph)
sources.body: Americans in 1898 told themselves they were going to war to free Cuba, and the Teller Amendment, which disclaimed any intention of annexing the island, gave that story legal form. Yet the map of what the United States actually kept tells a different story. Within months of the declaration of war, Congress annexed Hawaii by joint resolution, a step that had stalled since the overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani in 1893. The peace treaty with Spain then transferred Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines, none of which had figured in the public outcry over Cuban suffering. What linked these places was not sympathy but logistics. Steamships needed coal, telegraph cables needed landing points, and merchants anxious about access to China needed a navy that could reach Asian waters. The humanitarian crusade opened the door; a long-maturing commercial and naval strategy walked through it.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly support the author's argument about why the United States acquired territories in 1898?
facts: Secretary of State John Hay issued the Open Door notes in 1899 and 1900, calling for equal commercial access to China.

options.text: Secretary of State John Hay's Open Door notes of 1899 and 1900 called for equal trading access to China
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues that worry about reaching Asian, especially Chinese, markets drove the Pacific acquisitions. The Open Door notes show that soon after 1898 American policy did focus on commercial access to China.

options.text: Sensational newspaper stories in the Hearst and Pulitzer papers described Spanish cruelty toward Cuban civilians and stirred public demands for intervention
options.label: reversal
options.why: Yellow journalism backs the humanitarian story that the author plays down. It does not support the commercial and strategic explanation.

options.text: The Anti-Imperialist League, formed in 1898, drew members such as Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie, who denounced the annexation of the Philippines
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This shows opposition to annexation. It says nothing about the commercial and naval motives the author gives for the acquisitions.

options.text: The Dawes Severalty Act of 1887 divided reservation lands into individual allotments meant to push Native Americans toward farming and assimilation
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was domestic Indian policy. It has no bearing on why the United States took overseas territories in 1898.

items.stem: The Platt Amendment of 1901 could best be used to extend the author's argument by showing that the United States
facts: The Teller Amendment (1898) disclaimed any U.S. intention to annex Cuba.
The Platt Amendment (1901) limited Cuban sovereignty, gave the United States a right to intervene in Cuba, and provided for U.S. naval stations there, including Guantanamo Bay.

options.text: kept strategic control in Cuba, including naval bases, despite its pledge not to annex the island
options.label: key
options.why: The Platt Amendment gave the United States a right to intervene in Cuba and land for naval stations. It fits the author's claim that strategy, not sympathy, decided what the nation kept, even though the Teller Amendment had ruled out annexation.

options.text: withdrew entirely from Cuba once Spain was defeated, proving that sympathy for Cuban independence had been the main motive
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Platt Amendment did the opposite. It kept American influence in Cuba, so it cannot show a full withdrawal or a purely humanitarian motive.

options.text: extended United States citizenship to the residents of Cuba and created an elected legislature modeled on Congress
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Jones Act of 1917 gave citizenship to Puerto Ricans, not Cubans. The Platt Amendment did nothing of the kind.

options.text: declared through the Supreme Court that constitutional rights did not fully follow the flag into newly acquired islands
options.label: misattributed
options.why: That describes the Insular Cases, which were Supreme Court decisions. The Platt Amendment was a measure attached to an army appropriations bill and written into the Cuban constitution.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most relevant context for the long-maturing commercial and naval strategy described in the excerpt?
facts: The Panic of 1893 began a severe depression that heightened business interest in overseas markets for surplus American goods.
Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890) argued for naval power and overseas bases.

options.text: Business leaders' fears after the Panic of 1893 that domestic markets could not absorb American industrial output
options.label: key
options.why: The depression of the 1890s made many people believe that industrial overproduction called for foreign markets. That belief, together with calls for a larger navy, sits behind the strategy the author describes.

options.text: Rising alarm over German submarine attacks on neutral American merchant vessels crossing the Atlantic to trade with Britain
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: German submarine warfare against American shipping happened during the First World War, from 1915 to 1917. That was long after the strategy of the 1890s took shape.

options.text: Populist demands in the farm states for the free coinage of silver and government ownership of the railroads and telegraph lines
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Populist demands were real in the 1890s, but they concerned domestic money and regulation. They did not involve naval or commercial expansion overseas.

options.text: The Interstate Commerce Act's 1887 creation of a federal commission to regulate the railroad rates charged to shippers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This law regulated railroads inside the country. It did not shape the push for coaling stations and Asian markets.

items.stem: The acquisition of the Philippines described in the excerpt most directly led to which of the following developments in the years immediately following 1898?
facts: The Treaty of Paris (1898) transferred the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico from Spain to the United States.
The Philippine-American War was fought from 1899 to 1902 between U.S. forces and Filipino nationalists led by Emilio Aguinaldo.

options.text: A war from 1899 to 1902 between United States troops and Filipino forces seeking independence
options.label: key
options.why: Filipino nationalists under Emilio Aguinaldo resisted American rule after the Treaty of Paris. The result was the Philippine-American War.

options.text: The immediate grant of Philippine independence under the Treaty of Paris, after Filipino forces helped defeat Spain in Manila
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Treaty of Paris handed the Philippines to the United States. Independence came only in 1946.

options.text: The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1907, in which the government of the Philippines agreed to limit emigration of its laborers to California
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Gentlemen's Agreement was made with Japan and limited Japanese emigration. It had nothing to do with the Philippines.

options.text: A Japanese decision in 1941 to attack Pearl Harbor in direct retaliation for the American annexation of the Philippines four decades earlier
options.label: overstated
options.why: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor because of conflicts in 1941, including American oil embargoes and resistance to Japanese expansion. It was not direct revenge for an annexation made in 1898.

input.title: Debt, Taxes, and the Closing of the Courts: Shays' Rebellion and the Articles of Confederation

sources.title: A historian on the causes of Shays' Rebellion
sources.attribution: Miriam Okafor-Leland, historian, Courthouse Doors: Debt and Authority in Postwar New England, 2014 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a scholarly monograph on the early republic)
sources.body: The farmers who shut the county courts of western Massachusetts in the autumn of 1786 did not think of themselves as enemies of the Revolution. Many had served in the Continental Army, and their petitions used the language of 1776, protesting taxes laid without regard to a people's ability to pay. Their distress had layered causes. Boston merchants, pressed by British creditors after the war, called in debts from inland storekeepers, who in turn sued farmers. The state legislature, determined to retire its war debt, demanded taxes in hard money that hill towns simply did not have. Congress could offer no relief. It could not tax, could not regulate trade, and could not raise the troops to guard the Springfield arsenal; a militia paid for by private subscription did that in January 1787. To nationalists already pressing for reform, the episode proved the confederation was failing. The rebels wanted nearly the opposite: government closer to home and kinder to debtors.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's claim that the national government could offer no relief during the crisis described in the excerpt?
facts: Under the Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781), Congress could requisition funds from the states but could not levy taxes.
The First Bank of the United States was chartered in 1791 under the Constitution.
The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognized American independence and set the Mississippi River as the western boundary.

options.text: Congress could request funds from the states but had no power to levy taxes of its own.
options.label: key
options.why: The author argues Congress was powerless; the Articles denied Congress the power to tax, leaving it dependent on state requisitions that often went unpaid, so it had neither money nor troops to act.

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set up an orderly process for admitting new states from western lands.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The ordinance was real, but it was an accomplishment of the Confederation Congress and says nothing about its inability to respond to the debt crisis.

options.text: Congress created a national bank in 1791 to manage federal debts and issue a uniform paper currency.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The First Bank of the United States was chartered under the Constitution in 1791, after the Articles were replaced, so it cannot show Confederation weakness in 1786.

options.text: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence and set the Mississippi River as a western boundary.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The treaty ended the Revolutionary War; it does not show that Congress lacked the power to relieve debtors or put down unrest.

items.stem: The author's claim that the rebels wanted government closer to home and kinder to debtors would be most strengthened by evidence that
facts: Petitions and county conventions in western Massachusetts in 1786 called for paper money, debt relief, and moving the state legislature out of Boston.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) was a protest against Massachusetts state taxes and debt collection.

options.text: rebel petitions asked for paper money, relief for debtors, and moving the legislature out of Boston
options.label: key
options.why: County conventions and petitions in 1786 made these very demands, which match the author's claim that rebels sought government that was local and helped debtors.

options.text: rebel leaders called for a national convention to give Congress stronger powers over taxation and trade
options.label: reversal
options.why: Stronger central power was the nationalists' goal; the author says the rebels wanted nearly the opposite, so this evidence would undercut the claim.

options.text: rebel leaders sought arms and money from British officials in Canada to help them overthrow the state government
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The rebels mostly tried to close courts and win relief, not overthrow the state with British help, and evidence of that kind would not show a wish for responsive local government.

options.text: rebel town meetings demanded that the state constitution end slavery and guarantee voting rights to all men
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Slavery in Massachusetts had already been ended by court rulings in the early 1780s, and the rebels' grievances were about debt and taxes, not abolition or suffrage.

items.stem: The economic distress described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of
facts: After independence (1783) the United States lost the trade privileges it had enjoyed inside the British Empire, and a shortage of specie added to a postwar depression in the mid-1780s.
The Sugar Act (1764) and Stamp Act (1765) were British measures passed after the Seven Years' War.
The Embargo Act was passed in 1807.

options.text: a postwar depression marked by scarce hard currency and the loss of British imperial trade privileges
options.label: key
options.why: In the mid-1780s American merchants lost access to British imperial markets and owed British creditors, and specie ran short; this is the debt chain the excerpt describes.

options.text: British enforcement of the Sugar Act and Stamp Act after 1763, which drained scarce coin from colonial merchants and farmers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These were imperial taxes of the 1760s, two decades before the 1786 crisis, which came from state taxes and postwar debts.

options.text: runaway inflation as state governments printed huge amounts of paper money to repay creditors
options.label: reversal
options.why: Massachusetts refused to issue paper money and demanded hard money, so the farmers suffered from tight currency, not inflation.

options.text: the Embargo of 1807, which closed foreign markets to New England goods and left farmers unable to pay debts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Embargo Act came under Jefferson two decades later and had nothing to do with the crisis of 1786.

items.stem: Which later development was most similar to the events described in the excerpt in that rural citizens took up arms against a tax they considered unjust?
facts: In the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), western Pennsylvania farmers resisted the federal excise tax on whiskey passed in 1791.
Bacon's Rebellion took place in Virginia in 1676.
South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification (1832) declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void.

options.text: the Whiskey Rebellion, in which western Pennsylvania farmers resisted a federal excise tax
options.label: key
options.why: In 1794 backcountry farmers violently resisted Hamilton's 1791 whiskey excise, much as Massachusetts farmers resisted hard-money taxes, though this time the new federal government sent militia to put it down.

options.text: Bacon's Rebellion, in which Virginia frontier colonists attacked Native peoples and burned Jamestown
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Bacon's Rebellion happened in 1676, earlier rather than later, and grew mainly out of frontier conflict and anger at the governor's Indian policy, not taxes.

options.text: the Nullification Crisis, in which South Carolina's legislature declared the federal tariffs of 1828 and 1832 void
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Nullification was a state government's constitutional challenge to tariffs, not an armed uprising by farmers.

options.text: the Hartford Convention, in which New England Federalists protested the War of 1812 and proposed amendments
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Hartford Convention was a peaceful political meeting of Federalist leaders opposed to the war, not an armed rural revolt against taxes.

input.title: Upriver Trade at New Orleans, 1801-1810

sources.title: Flatboats and Keelboats from the Ohio and Upper Mississippi Valleys Recorded at the New Orleans Levee by Thibodeaux and Marsh, Commission Merchants, 1801-1810
sources.attribution: Annual tally kept by the fictional New Orleans commission house Thibodeaux and Marsh, which received western produce on consignment; ALTON-composed illustrative data, not real statistics (ALTON-composed, in the style of an early nineteenth-century merchant's yearly levee register)
sources.body: The table gives the number of upriver boats a fictional New Orleans merchant house recorded each year, along with the barrels of western flour it handled, from 1801 to 1810.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why the acquisition of the Louisiana Territory in 1803 mattered to the western farmers whose produce is recorded in the table?

options.text: It placed New Orleans under United States control, securing western farmers a dependable outlet for their crops
options.label: key
options.why: The boats in the table carried western produce down the Mississippi to New Orleans. Buying Louisiana from France in 1803 put the port under American control, so western trade no longer relied on Spanish or French permission.

options.text: It forced Great Britain to evacuate its forts in the Northwest Territory, opening the Ohio Valley to large-scale American settlement
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The British agreed to leave the Northwest forts in Jay's Treaty (1794). The Louisiana Purchase had nothing to do with it.

options.text: It removed Spain's claim to East and West Florida, giving western shippers new Gulf Coast ports at Mobile and Pensacola
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Spain gave up Florida in the Adams-Onis Treaty (1819), not in the 1803 purchase from France.

options.text: It funded a federal canal network that linked the Great Lakes to Atlantic ports and lowered freight rates for interior farmers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The purchase paid for no canals. The Erie Canal was a New York State project finished in 1825.

facts: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory, including New Orleans, from France.
Western farmers depended on the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans to get their produce to market in the early 1800s.

items.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the data in the table?

options.text: Upriver trade reaching New Orleans roughly doubled across the decade despite temporary setbacks
options.label: key
options.why: Boats went from 410 in 1801 to 820 in 1810, an increase of 100 percent. Flour went from 62 to 126 thousand barrels. Both numbers fell in 1803 and in 1808.

options.text: American control of New Orleans after 1803 caused a lasting decline in shipments from Ohio Valley farms
options.label: reversal
options.why: After 1803 shipments mostly went up. They reached 690 boats in 1806 and 820 in 1810.

options.text: By 1810 steam-powered vessels had replaced flatboats as the main carriers of western flour and pork down the river to the Gulf
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table records flatboats and keelboats only. Steamboats did not arrive at New Orleans until 1812, and they became common later than that.

options.text: Flour shipments rose steadily every year in the decade, unaffected by diplomatic disputes with European powers
options.label: overstated
options.why: Flour fell in 1803 and again in 1808, so the increase was not steady.

facts: Spain suspended the American right of deposit at New Orleans in 1802, which disrupted western trade until the 1803 purchase.
The first steamboat on the lower Mississippi, the New Orleans, reached New Orleans in 1812.

items.stem: The decline in recorded boats and flour between 1806 and 1808 shown in the table most likely reflected which of the following contexts?

options.text: A federal ban on American exports adopted in response to British and French seizures of neutral ships
options.label: key
options.why: Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807 banned American exports to foreign ports. Western flour was shipped out through New Orleans, so the embargo cut demand for it, and the 1808 numbers drop by 150 boats.

options.text: A British naval blockade of the Gulf Coast imposed during the war that the United States declared on Great Britain
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The War of 1812 began in 1812, after the 1808 decline.

options.text: A financial panic triggered when the Second Bank of the United States called in loans and tightened credit for western borrowers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Second Bank was chartered in 1816, and its credit tightening was linked to the Panic of 1819, which came about a decade after 1808.

options.text: A protective tariff passed by Congress that raised duties on imported manufactures to shield new New England textile mills
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The first protective tariff came in 1816. A tariff on imports also would not explain a drop in flour exports in 1808.

facts: Congress passed the Embargo Act in December 1807 in response to British and French interference with neutral American shipping.
The Embargo Act was repealed in 1809 and replaced by the Non-Intercourse Act.

items.stem: In the decade after the War of 1812, the territorial acquisition that expanded the trade shown in the table contributed most directly to which of the following developments?

options.text: Congressional conflict over admitting Missouri as a slave state, settled by the compromise of 1820
options.label: key
options.why: Missouri was carved out of the Louisiana Purchase. Its request to join the Union as a slave state set off a sectional crisis, which the Missouri Compromise of 1820 settled by drawing the 36 degrees 30 minutes line across the rest of the purchase.

options.text: The nullification crisis in which South Carolina rejected federal tariff laws passed in 1828 and 1832
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The nullification crisis was about tariff policy, not about land acquired in 1803. It also came after the decade the question asks about.

options.text: The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, which settled the disputed boundary between Maine and British Canada in 1842
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This treaty dealt with the border in the Northeast, not the Louisiana Territory, and it came much later.

options.text: The Gadsden Purchase, in which the United States bought land from Mexico in 1853 for a southern transcontinental railroad route
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Gadsden Purchase took place in 1853 and involved land bought from Mexico, not land from the Louisiana Purchase.

facts: Missouri, part of the Louisiana Purchase, applied to join the Union as a slave state in 1819.
The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, and it banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes.
